papers.citation: Du, Sun, Xu, Shah, Itkina, Song. Memory Anchors for Continual Robot Learning. arXiv:2608.26545 (preprint, Aug 2026).
papers.mechanism: Replay-based retention aimed at 'memory anchors'. These are old-task samples whose latents, in the old policy's observation embedding, overlap new-task observations while the old policy's action conflicts with the new task's action. Anchors are found once per new task with the previous policy in three steps: (1) k-means on latent distances keeps the overlapping cluster; (2) an action-disagreement test keeps points above mu+2sigma (the old policy denoises noised new-task actions); (3) the nearest old samples are retrieved. The replay buffer is then enriched with these anchors.
papers.setting: Imitation learning only, no RL. Diffusion policy (U-Net + ResNet-18) with experience replay on LIBERO; the pi0.5 VLA; a real robot (OpenJar, SweaterFold). Sequences of 3-10 tasks.
papers.results_vs_baselines: LIBERO-Goal NBT: 0.11 vs RandER 0.18, GSS 0.17, MIR 0.14. Removing the top 10% of anchors raises forgetting more than 4.5x (pi0.5: NBT 0.12 -> 0.35). Enriching the buffer with anchors cuts forgetting 63% on high-conflict pairs. On the real robot, 1.7x the success of RandER. No regularisation, LoRA or parameter-isolation baselines. No analysis of which parameters get overwritten: the paper only hypothesises 'interference in shared model resources'.
papers.relevance: This is the same structure our probe found: the conflict states (holding at the goal) sit on the old skill's densest latent region while the actions conflict, and the paper already turns that into a recipe in IL. The observation is therefore not novel for us. What remains open is RL with on-policy data and no demo buffer, retention without old-task data, and stage extension in a single network. It is a direct baseline: an anchor-weighted KL on the old head over the conflict states that our conflict_probe and done-probe already detect.

papers.citation: Kim, Lee, Narang, Guo. ACCRUE: Continual Off-Policy Reinforcement Learning for Robot Foundation Models. arXiv:2610.18596 (preprint, Oct 2026).
papers.mechanism: A frozen robot foundation model proposes an action chunk; its VLA base (GR00T N1.7 in sim, pi0.5 on DROID) is re-fine-tuned on cumulative demonstrations at each stage. One lightweight actor-critic is carried across all tasks: a small projector on frozen DINOv3 features plus proprioception that refines the reference chunk, with a ||a - a_ref||^2 penalty. Retention: before each stage, the previous actor's deterministic outputs are cached on the last N episodes of each finished task (N = 50-100 in sim, 20 on the real robot) and a lambda * L2 term pulls the actor toward them. The inherited critic trains only on current-task transitions. FastSAC in sim, FastTD3 on the real robot.
papers.setting: Isaac Lab contact-rich assembly: FORGE (peg insertion, gear meshing, nut threading; 3-stage sequences in 4 orderings) and AutoMate (5-stage plug-into-socket sequences). Real DROID robot on NIST board insertions and AutoMate parts.
papers.results_vs_baselines: FORGE NBT/AUC: ACCRUE 0.065/0.869, matching Isolated per-task checkpoints (AUC 0.868). Sequential 0.427/0.718, EWC 0.217/0.582, ER 0.518/0.697, RETAIN 0.514/0.682, Simple Recipe 0.038/0.583. AutoMate: ACCRUE 0.047/0.858 vs Sequential 0.178/0.792. Real robot: 31-68.5% less time to threshold with about 97% retention. Critic ablation: carrying it beats resetting (AUC 0.906 vs 0.890), and training it on old-task replay hurts (0.888).
papers.relevance: The closest published competitor for our a2r insert_key -> insert+turn stage: same simulator, contact-rich insertion, continual RL. It shows that 'one small shared actor + distillation to cached old outputs on a few retained episodes + carried critic' already reaches isolated-model AUC with about 5% forgetting. Our recipe must be compared against it and must differ on stated points: a scratch-RL PointNet PPO policy with no demos or VLA base, one network rather than a residual on a frozen base, ideally no retained old-task episodes, and handling of reversed skills.

papers.citation: Wolczyk et al. Fine-tuning Reinforcement Learning Models is Secretly a Forgetting Mitigation Problem. ICML 2024 (PMLR 235).
papers.mechanism: Diagnosis: fine-tuning a pre-trained RL policy forgets pre-trained capabilities (FPC) on states the agent does not reach early in fine-tuning (state-coverage gap) or that were poorly cloned (imperfect-cloning gap). Remedy: standard knowledge retention on the actor only, with the critic left unregularised: BC (KL to the pre-trained policy on 10k stored pre-training states), EWC (lambda = 100), or episodic memory.
papers.setting: SAC on Meta-World RoboticSequence (hammer -> push -> peg-unplug-side -> push-wall), where the pre-trained policy knows only the last two stages. Also NetHack (APPO) and Montezuma's Revenge (PPO).
papers.results_vs_baselines: Vanilla fine-tuning is virtually indistinguishable from training from scratch. BC is best (solves all four stages 80% of the time), then EM, then EWC. Forward transfer on the pre-trained stages (prefix 1): fine-tuning 0.18/0.28 (push-wall/peg-unplug-side), EWC 0.88/0.77, BC 0.93/0.92. With longer prefixes BC stays at 0.94-0.98 while fine-tuning falls to about 0. BC still works with only 100 stored states. CKA shows later layers drift most. NetHack SOTA rises from 5K to over 10K.
papers.relevance: Explains our 14-23-point drop. Stack keeps visiting Pick's early states but rewrites behaviour at the goal, and nothing anchors the old head's outputs, so the shared trunk drifts. It also sets the baseline to beat: full fine-tuning plus a small KL-to-old-expert term on old-skill states, which costs a few hundred PickCube envs in GPU sim. The literature predicts roughly full-FT speed with near-full retention for that baseline, so our partial-unit training has to beat it, not plain FT.

papers.citation: Kessler, Parker-Holder, Ball, Zohren, Roberts. Same State, Different Task: Continual Reinforcement Learning without Interference. AAAI 2022.
papers.mechanism: Separates interference (the same observation calls for different optimal actions across tasks) from forgetting. OWL: a shared feature extractor protected by EWC, one linear head per task for both actor and Q, and the replay buffer flushed at each new task. At test time an exponential-weights bandit picks the head from TD-error/reward feedback, so no task id is needed.
papers.setting: SAC on Pendulum with conflicting goals (+90/-90 degrees); a discrete-action Q-learning agent on MiniGrid (5 SimpleCrossing tasks, and SimpleCrossing + DoorKey); a MultiMNIST illustration.
papers.results_vs_baselines: Single-network shared-replay methods fail (MiniGrid SC: Exp Replay 0.01). OWL scores 0.85 with the true task id and 0.59 with bandit selection. Ablations: removing EWC from the trunk gives 0.45; replacing EWC with distillation of the old heads on current-task data also gives 0.45; full rehearsal reaches 0.99 (upper bound).
papers.relevance: Formalises our conflict states (holding at the goal: Pick holds, Stack releases) as interference that no single head can resolve; our per-skill heads already handle that part. What remains is trunk drift, and their ablation shows protecting the trunk matters (0.85 vs 0.45). It is also a warning: distilling old heads only on the new task's own data (LwF) underperformed EWC when task state sets differ. Old-data-free distillation therefore has to be tested, not assumed, although stage extension overlaps far more than their MiniGrid tasks.

papers.citation: Hu, Shim, Tang, Sung, Liu, Stone, Martin-Martin. Simple Recipe Works: Vision-Language-Action Models are Natural Continual Learners with Reinforcement Learning. RLC 2026 (Reinforcement Learning Journal).
papers.mechanism: Plain sequential fine-tuning with LoRA plus on-policy RL (GRPO on RLinf) on large pretrained VLAs. The authors attribute the low forgetting to three factors acting together: on-policy RL only reweights actions the policy already supports, a large pretrained model has low Fisher energy and a large near-null space, and LoRA restricts updates to low rank.
papers.setting: OpenVLA-OFT (main), pi0 and OpenVLA on LIBERO-Spatial/Object/Long, RoboCasa and ManiSkill, plus perturbation variants. Baselines: EWC, expert and dark replay, dynamic weight expansion, SLCA, RETAIN, and a multi-task oracle.
papers.results_vs_baselines: Seq. FT + LoRA keeps NBT at or below about 2% (LIBERO-Spatial: AVG 81.2%, NBT 0.3%, oracle 85.8%) and usually beats EWC, SLCA and RETAIN. Removing any one factor breaks it (LIBERO-Spatial): full FT instead of LoRA gives AVG 7.3% / NBT 40.9%; SFT instead of RL gives 29.9% / 78.7%; a 12M-parameter policy gives 13.1% / 11.4%. Fisher energy is 0.02 for OpenVLA-OFT vs 0.16 for the small policy.
papers.relevance: Our ManiSkill MLPs and the a2r PointNet + 512 residual trunk sit in their small-policy regime, where forgetting does not go away. The problem is therefore real for us and 'just use LoRA' does not answer it, but reviewers will still ask for a LoRA arm. Our measured full-FT update has rank 10-23 per layer, so LoRA at rank about 16 is the matched control. A trunk-width sweep would test their Fisher / null-space explanation in our setting.

papers.citation: Wolczyk, Zajac, Pascanu, Kucinski, Milos. Disentangling Transfer in Continual Reinforcement Learning. NeurIPS 2022.
papers.mechanism: Ablates which SAC components to carry between tasks (actor, critic, exploration, data) and combines the best choices into ClonEx-SAC: behavioural cloning (KL) of earlier actor heads on small saved buffers, applied to the actor only; best-return exploration (at task start, try every previous head and explore with the best one); multi-head actor and critic; no critic regularisation.
papers.setting: SAC on Continual World CW10/CW20 (Meta-World), plus 100 two-task pairs.
papers.results_vs_baselines: Final success 87% vs PackNet 80%; forward transfer 0.54 vs 0.18 (reference transfer 0.44-0.55). BC alone on CW10 (performance/forward transfer): 0.84/0.41, vs fine-tuning 0.10/0.31, PackNet 0.84/0.26, Perfect Memory 0.27/-1.13. In two-task transfer, the critic contributes most (0.20) vs actor 0.06 and exploration 0.09. Letting only the critic's head train gives -1.29. Any critic regularisation hurts (BC 0.82 -> 0.77). Exploring with old policies lifts EWC's CW20 forward transfer from -0.14 to 0.28; uniform-previous is nearly as good as best-return.
papers.relevance: Three direct lessons. (1) BC of the old head on old states does not cost forward transfer. (2) Keep the critic fully plastic and unregularised, never restricted to its head; wrwl/ppo.py already leaves the critic out of --freeze_trunk and --train_units. (3) Exploring with the old policy is an established transfer lever, which matches our finding that the floor is the main lever and local exploration ties global. Exploration belongs in the recipe but cannot be the claimed contribution.

papers.citation: Romer, Zhang, Schoellig. CLARE: Continual Learning for Vision-Language-Action Models via Autonomous Adapter Routing and Expansion. arXiv:2601.09512 (preprint, Jan 2026).
papers.mechanism: The pretrained policy stays frozen. At each expandable layer, autoencoder 'discriminators' score the new task's features: a new adapter is added only if every existing discriminator's reconstruction-error z-score exceeds gamma (feature novelty); otherwise the layer reuses an existing frozen adapter. At inference each layer routes to the adapter whose discriminator reconstructs best, so no task id is needed.
papers.setting: Imitation learning with a flow-matching DiT (about 200M parameters) pre-trained on LIBERO-90. 10-task LIBERO-Long/Goal/Spatial sequences, LIBERO-40, and an FR3 real robot. Baselines: SeqFFT, SeqLoRA, PackNet, ER, LOTUS, DMPEL, MLR.
papers.results_vs_baselines: LIBERO-Long AUC/FWT/NBT: CLARE 75.1/75.0/1.9 vs ER 60.5/76.6/22.7 and SeqFFT 22.4/76.1/74.7. Goal: 89.3/89.7/0.3. Spatial: 87.4/88.0/0.9. Cost is about 2% of VRAM per task. Expanding the observation-encoder side carries most of the benefit (AUC 65.4 vs 29.0 for decoder-only).
papers.relevance: The closest published mechanism for deciding where to unshare, but its criterion is input-feature novelty. Our probe shows the new skill's features lie 94-97% inside the old skill's subspace and the conflict is in the action mapping on familiar states, so a CLARE-style novelty test would mark Pick->Stack as 'share everything'. A conflict-based criterion (old-head vs new-target action disagreement on overlapping states, as in Memory Anchors) is the variant that would differentiate us, and CLARE is the baseline it must beat.

papers.citation: Shenfeld, Pari, Agrawal. RL's Razor: Why Online Reinforcement Learning Forgets Less. ICLR 2026.
papers.mechanism: Among the many solutions to a new task, on-policy RL converges to ones that stay KL-close to the base policy. Forgetting is predicted by the forward KL between the fine-tuned and base policy, measured on the new task's distribution. An oracle SFT on KL-minimal labels forgets even less than RL.
papers.setting: LLMs (GRPO), ParityMNIST, and OpenVLA-7B in SimplerEnv (pick-can trained with REINFORCE; forgetting measured on drawer tasks).
papers.results_vs_baselines: Forward KL predicts forgetting with R^2 0.96 on MNIST and 0.71 on LLMs. Parameter-space measures do much worse: weight-change L1 0.34, Fisher-weighted L2 0.58, spectral norm 0.58, activation change 0.52-0.55. All updates were full rank; the apparent sparsity came from bfloat16.
papers.relevance: Gives a principled reason for two of our results: choosing units by importance or conflict does no better than random, and the low rank of the FT update was no more concentrated than a random-target control. Parameter-space locality does not predict damage; change in the output distribution does. It argues for protection in function space (a KL on the old head over the states that matter) while leaving shared parameters free, which restates the 'conflict lives in shared parameters' intuition as a loss.

papers.citation: Ahn, Hyeon, Oh, Hwang, Moon. Prevalence of Negative Transfer in Continual Reinforcement Learning: Analyses and a Simple Baseline (Reset & Distill). ICLR 2025.
papers.mechanism: For each new task: reset the online actor and critic and learn the task from scratch with SAC or PPO. Then distill into a persistent offline actor, with a KL to the new expert on freshly generated expert rollouts plus a KL to earlier experts on small stored buffers (10k samples per task).
papers.setting: Meta-World sequences of 8 tasks (Easy, Hard, Random) with SAC and PPO, plus pairwise transfer across Meta-World task groups.
papers.results_vs_baselines: Negative transfer is common, worse with PPO than SAC, and not fixed by plasticity remedies (ReDo, InFeR, CReLU, Wasserstein regularisation). Hard sequence, SAC transfer/forgetting: FT -0.500/0.504, EWC -0.457/0.512, P&C -0.507/0.472, ClonEx -0.513/0.005, R&D -0.041/0.008. With PPO, R&D reaches +0.025/0.029 while P&C diverged.
papers.relevance: Our PullCube-from-Push case (scratch 1.2M steps vs >7M or never with any reuse) is exactly their negative transfer, and ClonEx-style retention does not fix it. An RSI recipe needs a reuse-or-reset switch. R&D always resets; a cheaper option is a short race between a fresh learner and the reused one, then distilling the winner into the shared network while the old heads stay protected by the same distillation.

papers.citation: Yang, Zhou, Jiang, Long, Shi. Continual Task Allocation in Meta-Policy Network via Sparse Prompting (CoTASP). ICML 2023.
papers.mechanism: At each hidden layer, an over-complete dictionary maps a task embedding (Sentence-BERT of the task text) to a sparse prompt via lasso; positive coefficients select the neurons that form the task's sub-network. A weight gets zero gradient only if both its input and output neurons were used by earlier tasks, so new tasks share neurons with similar old tasks and learn in unused ones. The dictionary is refit after each task, and nothing is replayed.
papers.setting: SAC on Continual World CW10/CW20. Single-head actor (4x1024 MLP); the critic is retrained for each task.
papers.results_vs_baselines: CW10 performance 0.92 with forgetting 0.00; CW20 0.88 with 0.00. Compare PackNet 0.80/0.78, EWC 0.64/0.60, fine-tuning 0.12/0.05 (forgetting 0.70/0.72), and ClonEx-SAC 0.86/0.87 as reported by its authors.
papers.relevance: The most direct published form of 'share the neurons a similar old skill uses, train only new ones', and the mechanism our 5%/20% train_units runs approximate. The details differ in an important way: CoTASP selects neurons by task similarity and freezes only old-to-old connections, while our row masks freeze whole units. Our importance = random result suggests the gains come from capacity and gating rules rather than from clever unit choice. It is a required baseline if we keep a parameter-isolation arm.

papers.citation: Wolczyk, Zajac, Pascanu, Kucinski, Milos. Continual World: A Robotic Benchmark for Continual Reinforcement Learning. NeurIPS 2021.
papers.mechanism: A benchmark plus a standardised SAC evaluation of continual-learning methods: fine-tuning, L2, EWC, MAS, VCL, PackNet, Perfect Memory, A-GEM and multi-task. Metrics are performance, forgetting and forward transfer, with a reference-transfer upper bound. The actor is multi-head and CL regularisation is applied to the actor only.
papers.setting: SAC on CW10/CW20 sequences of Meta-World manipulation tasks, 1M steps per task.
papers.results_vs_baselines: CW20 performance/forgetting/forward transfer: fine-tuning 0.05/0.73/0.20; L2 0.43/0.02/-0.71; EWC 0.60/0.02/-0.17; MAS 0.51; VCL 0.48; PackNet 0.80/0.00/0.19; Perfect Memory 0.12; A-GEM 0.07/0.71. Multi-task scores 0.51 (0.65 with PopArt); reference transfer is 0.46. Regularising the critic is harmful, and most methods kill forward transfer.
papers.relevance: Supplies the baseline set and metrics reviewers expect; our steps-to-90% maps onto its forward transfer. Its central finding mirrors ours: regularisation or isolation (EWC, L2, PackNet, which resembles our frozen units) keeps old skills but loses transfer and speed, while fine-tuning transfers but forgets. Closing that gap is the target; BC/ClonEx later did so with old-task data.

papers.citation: Yadav, Zhou, Wagenmaker, Pertsch, Levine. Robust Finetuning of Vision-Language-Action Robot Policies via Parameter Merging (RETAIN). ICLR 2026.
papers.mechanism: Post-hoc weight interpolation theta = (1 - alpha) * theta_pre + alpha * theta_ft, optionally with a separate alpha per module (vision, language, action expert). Sequential skills are added by fine-tuning from the previous merged model and merging again.
papers.setting: pi0-FAST-DROID on real DROID tasks (whiteboard wiping, plates into a rack) and pi0 on LIBERO (pot-on-stove, mugs-on-plates, items-into-basket), with about 45-100 demos per task. Fine-tuning is SFT, not RL.
papers.results_vs_baselines: Generalist performance stays about equal to the pretrained model, with competitive in-distribution success and higher OOD success on the new task (above 60% on plates and about 80% on whiteboard OOD, vs 30-50% for baselines; about 40% above prior fine-tuning methods on real robots). Only the language backbone needs interpolation (best alpha_l about 0.8). However, ACCRUE (2026) found it forgets heavily in small shared RL actors (FORGE NBT 0.514 vs 0.427 for sequential).
papers.relevance: A zero-training-cost baseline we can run on existing Pick->Stack checkpoints: sweep alpha and plot Stack success against PickCube retention through the old head. Our full-FT update moves the hidden weights only 11-13%, so interpolation is a fair Pareto reference. ACCRUE's small-actor result predicts it will not beat distillation, which would itself be useful evidence.

papers.citation: Gaya, Doan, Caccia, Soulier, Denoyer, Raileanu. Building a Subspace of Policies for Scalable Continual Learning (CSP). ICLR 2023 (oral).
papers.mechanism: Policies live in the convex hull of anchor weight vectors. For each new task, add an anchor initialised at the mean of the existing anchors and train it with Dirichlet-sampled mixtures. Keep the anchor only if the best mixture's estimated value beats the old subspace's best by more than 10% (W(alpha_new) > 1.1 W(alpha_old)); otherwise prune it. Each task stores only its alpha; the critic and buffer are reset per task, with no replay.
papers.setting: SAC on Brax locomotion (HalfCheetah, Ant, Humanoid; 4-8-task scenarios) and Continual World CW10.
papers.results_vs_baselines: Brax normalised performance 1.27/1.11/1.76 (HalfCheetah/Ant/Humanoid) with 3.4-5.4 anchors, vs PackNet 0.85/1.08/0.96, EWC 0.43/0.55/0.94, PNN 1.03/0.98/0.98 (4-8 columns) and FT-N 1.16/0.97/0.65. Zero forgetting by design. CW10: 0.81 with 5.3 heads vs PackNet 0.83 with 10.
papers.relevance: A clean published rule for adding capacity only when the old subspace is not enough, based on a value test. For the RSI framing it is the reference for deciding when a new skill fits inside the old skill's span and when it needs new parameters: Pick->Stack likely fits, Push->Pull likely does not. Its anchor/alpha storage also keeps the old policy exactly while sharing almost all weights.

papers.citation: Wang et al. Sparse Diffusion Policy: A Sparse, Reusable, and Flexible Policy for Robot Learning. CoRL 2024.
papers.mechanism: Mixture-of-experts layers inside a transformer diffusion policy, with task-specific routers. For a new task, all old experts, routers and non-MoE modules are frozen and new experts (8 per task, 2 active) plus a new router are added. Old tasks stay untouched, and new tasks can still route to old experts.
papers.setting: Imitation learning. Continual robomimic sequence Can -> Lift -> Square; ablations on MimicGen Stack -> Hammer Cleanup -> Coffee.
papers.results_vs_baselines: Full fine-tuning forgets completely (Can 0.97 -> 0.00 after Lift) while reaching 0.89 on Square. SDP keeps Can at 0.94 and Lift at 1.00, with Square 0.75, at about 9.2M active parameters. LoRA keeps 0.94/1.00 with Square 0.73, but its active parameters grow from 9.0M to 14.9M.
papers.relevance: Shows the same trade-off we measured: isolation keeps old skills while new-skill success or speed drops (0.75 vs 0.89 here; 2.2M vs 1.5M steps for us). It is the MoE form of 'train only what the new skill needs while reusing old modules through a router', and a useful architecture-level baseline if the a2r stage uses a transformer. For an MLP trunk the equivalent is new units read only by the new head, which interfere with nothing by construction.

papers.citation: Liu, Zhang, Asadi, Liu, Zhao, Sabach, Fakoor. TAIL: Task-specific Adapters for Imitation Learning with Large Pretrained Models. ICLR 2024.
papers.mechanism: A frozen pretrained decision model (CLIP encoders + GPT-2 temporal decoder with FiLM) gets one small adapter per task. Compares LoRA (on q/v and FFN), bottleneck adapters, prefix tuning and RoboAdapter against full fine-tuning, EWC and experience replay.
papers.setting: Imitation learning on LIBERO: pretrain on 40 Kitchen tasks, then adapt sequentially to the Spatial, Goal, Object, Living Room and Study Room suites and to LIBERO-10, with 40 training demos per task.
papers.results_vs_baselines: LIBERO-10: LoRA reaches FWT 0.70 with zero backward forgetting, vs full FT 0.48 FWT / -0.55 BWT, ER 0.45/-0.49 and EWC 0.30/-0.43. Prefix 0.51, bottleneck 0.46, RoboAdapter 0.42. LoRA uses 1.17% of the parameters (7.8MB per task vs 28GB of replay data).
papers.relevance: Adapter-per-skill is the zero-forgetting reference every 'same network' claim will be compared with. Note that LoRA beat full FT on new-task performance there (large pretrained model, small demo sets), whereas in our RL setting full FT is fastest. The paper should state this regime difference (pretraining scale, IL vs RL) explicitly.

takeaways: Verdict on 'what to share, where to unshare'. The problem is timely: four closely related 2026 papers (CLARE in January, Simple Recipe at RLC, Memory Anchors in August, ACCRUE in October). The parameter-locality version of the claim is not supported. Three lines of evidence point the same way: (1) our own data, where units chosen by importance or conflict do no better than random and the FT update is low rank but no more concentrated than a random-target control, spread over about 190/256 units; (2) RL's Razor, where weight- and activation-change measures predict forgetting with R^2 0.34-0.58 vs 0.96 for forward KL; (3) Continual World and LIBERO, where isolation such as PackNet keeps old skills but loses transfer. Go only with a function-space claim: protect the old head's outputs on the few states that matter and let all shared parameters move. Report unit masking as a baseline or negative result.

Run this control first, because it decides the paper. Full fine-tuning plus the exploration floor plus KL(old head on the new trunk || frozen Pick expert), with three state sources: (a) a slice of the GPU envs running PickCube, as in ClonEx/ACCRUE (upper bound); (b) only the new task's own PPO minibatch states, as in LwF / Progress & Compress, with no old data or env; (c) only the conflict/anchor states found by conflict_probe or the done-probe, as in Memory Anchors. This is a few lines in wrwl/ppo.py. The literature predicts (a) reaches about the 1.5M steps of full FT with retention near 0.99 (Wolczyk 2024: BC forward transfer 0.92-0.98 vs at most 0.28 for FT; ClonEx: BC costs no transfer; ACCRUE: NBT 0.05-0.07 at isolated-model AUC). If (b) or (c) match (a), the defensible claim is old-data-free retention for stage-extension RL. OWL found current-data distillation weak (0.45 vs 0.85 with EWC) when task states differ, so this is a real test, not a given.

Novelty boundaries to state in the extended abstract. Conflict states sitting where new observations collapse onto the old skill's latents is Memory Anchors' finding (IL, needs stored old data). One small actor-critic carried across tasks, distilled toward cached old outputs on retained episodes, with the critic carried over, is ACCRUE (Isaac Lab FORGE/AutoMate insertion; needs stored old episodes, and its VLA base is re-fine-tuned on cumulative demos). Adding parameters only where features are novel is CLARE. LoRA plus on-policy RL barely forgetting is Simple Recipe (large VLAs only). In our searches no paper does RL stage extension (old skill = prefix of the new one) in a single scratch-RL policy without old-task data, and none gates reuse vs reset for reversed skills. Those are the open slots.

Input-subspace protection will probably starve learning here. GPM/Adam-NSCL-style projection removes the old activation subspace from each trunk layer's update, but 94-97% of the new skill's activation energy lies inside that subspace. The new head trains freely while the trunk can use only the 3-6% residual, so expect a speed close to output-layer-only (3.1M steps). Scaled projection is the family to try if a parameter-space arm is wanted: SGP (AAAI 2023, arXiv 2302.01386, includes Atari RL) and TRGP (ICLR 2022, arXiv 2202.02931). A one-day run turns the occupancy measurement into a falsifiable prediction instead of an analysis section.

Critic: keep one critic per skill, initialised from the old critic, fully plastic and unregularised. Evidence: in Continual World, critic regularisation hurts. In ClonEx, the critic carries most of the transfer (0.20 vs 0.06 for the actor) and a head-only critic gives -1.29. In ACCRUE, carrying the critic beats resetting it, and training it on old-task replay hurts. wrwl/ppo.py already leaves the critic outside --freeze_trunk and --train_units; keep the same rule in the a2r port.

Exploration: exploring with the old policy is a known transfer lever. In ClonEx, best-return exploration lifts EWC's CW20 forward transfer from -0.14 to 0.28, and uniform-previous is nearly as good. This matches our results that the floor is the main lever and that local exploration ties global. Keep the floor in the recipe and in every baseline (the plan review already called unfloored baselines unfair), but do not claim it as the contribution.

Reversed skills need a reuse-or-reset switch. Reset & Distill shows negative transfer is common, worse with PPO, and fixed neither by plasticity remedies (ReDo, InFeR, CReLU) nor by ClonEx; reset plus distill fixes it (Hard-sequence transfer -0.04 vs about -0.5). Our PullCube case (scratch 1.2M vs reuse >7M) is the demo. Cheap gates exist: CSP keeps new capacity only if value improves by more than 10%; CompoNet (ICML 2024, arXiv 2506.14811) falls back to its own internal policy when old modules are irrelevant; or race a fresh learner against the reused one for about 0.3M steps and distill the winner into the shared network under the same old-head KL.

Size regime and framing. Simple Recipe's protection needs a large pretrained model: a 12M-parameter policy forgets (NBT 11.4% on LIBERO-Spatial) and full FT forgets badly (40.9%). Our ManiSkill MLPs and the a2r PointNet + 512 trunk are in that small regime, so the forgetting is real and 'use LoRA on a big VLA' does not dissolve the problem. Say so up front, but still include LoRA at rank about 16 (the measured full-FT update is rank 10-23 per layer). A trunk-width sweep would check their Fisher-energy explanation in our setting.

Baselines and metrics reviewers will expect: fine-tuning with the floor; EWC on the actor; PackNet or our 5-20% train_units; LoRA at rank about 16; a RETAIN alpha-sweep on existing Stack checkpoints (free, though ACCRUE found it forgets in small shared RL actors: FORGE NBT 0.514); ClonEx-style BC on old states; ACCRUE-style last-N-episode distillation; CLARE- or CoTASP-style expansion or masking; and R&D for the reversed pair. Report AUC, forward transfer and NBT (Continual World / LIBERO / ACCRUE conventions) alongside steps-to-90% and old-head retention, with at least 3 seeds and confidence intervals. Plot the speed-vs-retention Pareto, because every isolation method above trades new-skill speed for retention (SDP 0.75 vs FFT 0.89 on Square; our 2.2M vs 1.5M steps).

Do not rely on two-task pairs alone for the RSI claim. ClonEx found BC neutral for transfer on pairs but clearly positive on 10-20-task sequences. Wolczyk 2024 found that fine-tuning's transfer on the pre-trained stages falls from 0.18 to about 0 as the new-stage prefix grows. Show at least one 3-4-skill chain in ManiSkill before the a2r insert -> insert+turn pair, keeping one head per skill and the old-head KL for every earlier skill. The cost grows linearly with the number of old heads; Progress & Compress's online EWC is the constant-cost reference.

Other confirmed work for the related-work section: CLEAR (NeurIPS 2019, arXiv 1811.11682: replay plus behavioural cloning to the past self); Policy Consolidation (ICML 2019, arXiv 1902.00255: multi-timescale KL cascade); Progress & Compress (ICML 2018, arXiv 1805.06370: compresses without stored old data via distillation plus online EWC, the closest precedent for option (b)); LIBERO (NeurIPS 2023 Datasets & Benchmarks, arXiv 2306.03310: sequential fine-tuning had the best forward transfer, and PackNet's capacity split hurt it); M2Distill (ICRA 2025, arXiv 2410.00064); IsCiL (NeurIPS 2024, arXiv 2410.22658); DMPEL (arXiv 2506.05985); PSEC (ICLR 2025, arXiv 2502.05932); iManip (ICCV 2025, arXiv 2503.07087); LEGION (Nature Machine Intelligence 2025); modulating masks (TMLR 2023, arXiv 2212.11110); Progressive Neural Networks (arXiv 1606.04671).

papers.citation: Sen Lin, Li Yang, Deliang Fan, Junshan Zhang. Beyond Not-Forgetting: Continual Learning with Backward Knowledge Transfer (CUBER). NeurIPS 2022.
papers.mechanism: Before training each new task t, CUBER runs two tests per layer and per old task j on one batch. (1) Sufficient projection: ||Proj_Sj(g_t)|| >= eps1·||g_t||, with eps1 = 0.5 and at most 2 old tasks per layer. (2) Positive correlation: cos(g_j(w_j), g_t(w_{t-1})) >= eps2, with eps2 = 0 in the main table. Here g_j is the old task's gradient stored at the end of its training, so no replay is needed. The tests sort old tasks into three regimes. Regime 1 (weak projection): plain GPM orthogonal projection. Regime 2 (strong projection, conflicting gradients): orthogonal projection plus a TRGP-style learned scaling matrix inside S_j. Regime 3 (strong projection, aligned gradients): the shared weights may move inside S_j, under a penalty lambda·||Proj_Sj(w - w_{t-1})||. The Regime-3 alignment test is re-run every iteration, and a task is permanently demoted to Regime 2 the first time it fails. Theorems: under positive correlation, unconstrained steps move toward the joint optimum and do not raise the old loss.
papers.setting: Supervised task-incremental continual learning on a fixed-capacity network, no replay. Benchmarks: PMNIST (3-layer MLP, shared head), 10-split CIFAR-100 (5-layer AlexNet), 5-Datasets and 20-split MiniImageNet (reduced ResNet-18), multi-head.
papers.results_vs_baselines: ACC/BWT (%): CIFAR-100 75.54/+0.13 vs TRGP 74.46/-0.9 and GPM 72.48/-0.9. MiniImageNet 62.67/+0.23 vs 61.78/-0.5 and 60.41/-0.7. PMNIST 97.25/-0.02 vs 96.34/-0.8 and 93.91/-3. 5-Datasets 93.48/0.00 vs TRGP 93.56/-0.04. First replay-free, fixed-capacity method with positive BWT. Forward transfer over GPM: +2.79 vs TRGP +2.01 on CIFAR-100, credited to relaxing the constraint inside selected old subspaces. On an overlapping-class sequence it picked the truly related old task in most cases (BWT +0.28 vs TRGP -0.18).
papers.relevance: The clearest template for 'open the old skill's subspace only where sharing helps', with an explicit layer-wise decision rule. Your numbers put Pick deep in the sufficient-projection regime in every layer: 94-97% of Stack's activation energy inside Pick's subspace gives a projection ratio of about 0.97-0.98, far above 0.5. So the alignment test is what decides. Two parts break under PPO. First, the stored end-of-training gradient of a converged RL expert is mostly noise. Second, your step-to-step conflict oscillation would trip the one-shot demotion almost immediately. RL adaptation: use the gradient of a retention loss (KL or BC of the old head on fresh old-skill states from sim) as g_j, recompute it each iteration, and smooth the test (EMA over PPO epochs) instead of demoting permanently.

papers.citation: Sen Lin, Li Yang, Deliang Fan, Junshan Zhang. TRGP: Trust Region Gradient Projection for Continual Learning. ICLR 2022 (spotlight).
papers.mechanism: Shared weights still update only orthogonal to all old input subspaces (GPM bases). Per layer, TRGP selects a 'trust region' of old tasks with ||Proj_Sj(grad L_t)|| >= eps_l·||grad L_t||. Settings: eps_l = 0.5, top-K = 2 by projection norm; K = 1 already gives a clear gain. Each selected old task gets a private scaled weight projection for the new task: W_eff = W + sum_j [W B_j Q_jt B_j^T - W B_j B_j^T]. B_j are the old bases and Q_jt is a k x k matrix (identity init), learned jointly with W and stored per task and layer. Old tasks keep using the frozen projection W B_j B_j^T, so the function they rely on never changes.
papers.setting: Supervised continual learning: PMNIST, 10-split CIFAR-100, CIFAR-100 superclass, 5-Datasets, 20-split MiniImageNet; same architectures as GPM.
papers.results_vs_baselines: ACC/BWT (%) vs GPM: PMNIST 96.34/-0.8 vs 93.91/-3. CIFAR-100 74.46/-0.9 vs 72.48/-0.9. 5-Datasets 93.56/-0.04 vs 91.22/-1. MiniImageNet 61.78/-0.5 vs 60.41/-0.7. Also beats OWM, EWC, HAT, A-GEM and ER. Training time is about 1.2-1.65x GPM. Extra memory is one k x k matrix per selected (task, layer).
papers.relevance: This is 'reuse the old representation, unshare inside it' in its cleanest form. The new skill gets a private re-weighting of exactly the directions Pick occupies (k = 10 at the input and about 20 in hidden layers, so a few hundred to about 1k private parameters per skill). Shared weights learn only in the free space. It is the most direct way to handle your conflict states (hold vs release on Pick's densest directions) without touching Pick. Limitation: Q only re-mixes outputs within the span of W·B_j. A freer variant is a private adapter whose input side is fixed to Pick's bases and whose output side is free. Testable prediction: retention near your output-only arm (0.99), with speed between output-only (3.1M) and full FT (1.5M). Requires a skill ID at test time.

papers.citation: Gobinda Saha, Kaushik Roy. Continual Learning with Scaled Gradient Projection (SGP). AAAI 2023.
papers.mechanism: Keeps GPM's per-layer bases from the SVD of input representations (energy threshold). Each basis gets an importance lambda_i = (alpha+1)·sigma_i / (alpha·sigma_i + max sigma), computed from its singular value. The update is g - M·Lambda·M^T·g, so the step along basis i is scaled by (1 - lambda_i) instead of removed. The top direction is fully frozen, and low-energy old directions stay mostly open. Importances accumulate across tasks, capped at 1. Old-basis singular values are re-estimated from projections of the new task's representations, so no old data is needed. alpha -> infinity recovers GPM. Opening rule: by old-task energy alone.
papers.setting: Supervised: 10-split CIFAR-100, 20-split miniImageNet, CIFAR-100 superclass. Continual RL: PPO (3 conv layers + 1024-unit FC), 6 sequential Atari games x 10M steps each, eps_th = 0.995, alpha = 25, 3 seeds.
papers.results_vs_baselines: CIFAR-100 ACC 76.05 vs GPM 72.48, TRGP 74.46 and FS-DGPM 74.33 (BWT about -1%). miniImageNet 62.83 vs 60.41 (GPM) and 60.93 (TRGP). Forward transfer about +4-5 points over GPM. Even after 20 tasks, only about 18-37% of stored directions are fully blocked. RL: accumulated normalized reward is 12% above GPM and 36% above BLIP; plain fine-tuning hovers near 1 of a possible 6. Extra memory is about 0.1% over GPM, vs about 10x for TRGP. Important detail: in RL, feeding projected gradients into Adam caused catastrophic forgetting, so they project Adam's output step instead.
papers.relevance: The only subspace-projection paper with an on-policy (PPO) continual-RL experiment. Its single knob, alpha, traces the curve between your output-only arm (alpha -> infinity) and full FT. It plugs directly onto the bases occupancy_test.py already computes. Caveat for your data: SGP protects the highest-energy directions hardest, and your conflict states sit exactly there. So expect it mainly to speed up learning in the post-release new territory, and pair it with a private map (TRGP's Q) for the conflict region. The Adam finding applies directly to wrwl/ppo.py: project the optimizer's step, not the gradient.

papers.citation: Jiaqi Wang, Zhou Fang, Qiongfeng Shi, Yi Zhou. OrthoSkillVLA: Continual Skill Learning via Gradient-Informed Skill Subspace Adaptation. PRCV 2026 (arXiv:2608.19589, Aug 2026).
papers.mechanism: Each new skill gets a LoRA (r = 64). Its down-projection is frozen and set to the top singular vectors of the skill's accumulated gradient, after projecting out the basis of earlier skills. The gradient x^T·delta serves as a proxy for the feature subspace the skill occupies. Only the up-projection is trained. The basis then grows by the new skill's directions up to an energy threshold eps. Budgets differ by module: loose for the VLM backbone (eps = 0.99, keeps plasticity) and very strict for the action head (eps = 0.9999, protects 'localized velocity patterns'). The output decoder is a frozen base plus a tiny expert per skill. A training-free router picks the skill whose decoder-gradient subspace captures the most feature energy.
papers.setting: Imitation learning without demo replay, on X-VLA (about 0.9B parameters). Simulation: a skill-incremental LIBERO-100 protocol (OpenClose, PickPlace and Turn skills; 3 skill orders). Real robot: xArm with a dexterous hand (Flip, Pick, Push, Press; 20 trials each).
papers.results_vs_baselines: Final success rate / negative backward transfer: 83.50 / 0.13 vs KeepLoRA 56.61 / 0.46, IncLoRA 34.11 / 0.83, SeqLoRA 32.44 / 0.89, O-LoRA 30.50 / 0.85, EWC 25.17 / 0.68. Ablation: separate thresholds alone 60.44; MoE decoder alone 67.94; both 83.50. Raising the head threshold from 0.99 to 0.9999 lifts SR from 59.8 to 84.8. The training-free router gets 83.5 vs 86.2 with oracle routing. Real robot: 86.25 vs 71.25 for KeepLoRA.
papers.relevance: The closest robotics prior work, and the one an RSS reviewer will cite against your a2r/VLA stage. Its two findings match yours. First, protection must be much stricter near the action output (your last hidden layer is the most occupied, 58/256). Second, private per-skill output capacity carries much of the gain (your output-only arm retains 0.992). It does not address RL, exploration, or stage-extension conflict states, which leaves room for your contribution. Its gradient-subspace allocation is a ready-made baseline for 'which directions to give the new skill'.

papers.citation: Mehrdad Farajtabar, Navid Azizan, Alex Mott, Ang Li. Orthogonal Gradient Descent for Continual Learning (OGD). AISTATS 2020.
papers.mechanism: Protects old outputs rather than old inputs. For about 200 stored samples per old task, it keeps the gradient of the model's output with respect to all parameters (the ground-truth-logit variant, OGD-GTL). These gradients are orthogonalized by Gram-Schmidt, and their components are removed from every new-task gradient. To first order the old predictions do not change. Parameters remain free to move in any direction that leaves those outputs unchanged, including directions that old activations use.
papers.setting: Supervised, small MLPs: permuted, rotated and split MNIST; SGD with lr 1e-3.
papers.results_vs_baselines: Split MNIST task-1 accuracy 98.6 vs A-GEM 92.9, EWC 90.2, SGD 88.2. Rotated MNIST task 1: 75.6 vs 72.6 / 61.9 / 62.9. On permuted MNIST it is roughly on par with A-GEM (task 1: 79.5 vs 85.5) and well ahead of EWC and SGD. Stated limitations: memory grows with the number of tasks, large learning rates break the first-order argument, and only SGD was tested (Adam left to future work).
papers.relevance: The function-space alternative to GPM, and the one that matches your retention protocol. You only need Pick's old head output (8 action means) unchanged on Pick states, not every Pick activation direction. GPM would freeze every direction Pick's activations use in each shared layer (10 at the input, about 20 in hidden layers), and those directions hold 94-97% of Stack's input energy. An output-Jacobian constraint removes at most 8 x N_states parameter directions and lets the trunk move wherever Pick's head is blind. In sim, the 'stored gradients' can be recomputed every PPO iteration from fresh expert rollouts, which fixes OGD's drift and memory issues. We found no on-policy RL paper doing this.

papers.citation: Junfeng Fang, Houcheng Jiang, Kun Wang, Yunshan Ma, Jie Shi, Xiang Wang, Xiangnan He, Tat-Seng Chua. AlphaEdit: Null-Space Constrained Knowledge Editing for Language Models. ICLR 2025 (Outstanding Paper).
papers.mechanism: Builds K0 from the keys (layer inputs) of about 100k preserved Wikipedia facts and eigendecomposes K0·K0^T. Eigenvectors with eigenvalue above 1e-2 are dropped, and every edit perturbation is projected onto the remaining null space (P = U_hat·U_hat^T). Then (W + Delta·P)·K0 = W·K0 exactly, so preserved outputs are provably unchanged. The closed-form solution adds a term that protects previously edited keys during sequential editing. P is computed once and reused for all edits. Opening rule: a fixed eigenvalue cut on the covariance of preserved inputs.
papers.setting: Sequential locate-then-edit on LLaMA3-8B, GPT-J and GPT2-XL. Edits: Counterfact and ZsRE (2,000 edits in batches of 100). General ability: GLUE-style tasks and MMLU.
papers.results_vs_baselines: LLaMA3 on Counterfact, efficacy / generalization / specificity: 98.90 / 94.22 / 67.88 vs MEMIT 65.65 / 64.65 / 51.56. Adding only the projection to existing editors improves them by 36.7% on average. General capability holds at the original level after 3,000 edits, while baselines collapse after about 2,000.
papers.relevance: The strongest recent evidence that you can add capability to the same weights while leaving preserved inputs' outputs exactly unchanged, at scale and in one line of code. Mapping: keys = Pick-state activations, edit = Stack. The catch shows why your problem is harder. AlphaEdit's new keys mostly lie outside the preserved key space in a wide layer, while yours do not (94-97% overlap in 256-d layers). So a hard null space will starve Stack, and the real question is how to change outputs on the overlapping part. That points to function-space protection (OGD) or private parameters (TRGP) rather than a stricter null space.

papers.citation: Guanxiong Zeng, Yang Chen, Bo Cui, Shan Yu. Continual learning of context-dependent processing in neural networks (OWM + CDP). Nature Machine Intelligence, 2019.
papers.mechanism: OWM (orthogonal weight modification) projects each layer's update with P = I - A(A^T A + alpha·I)^{-1} A^T over previously seen inputs A. P is updated recursively, as in recursive least squares, so no data is stored. alpha softens the projection, and the paper suggests a larger alpha or a forgetting factor when capacity runs out. The CDP (context-dependent processing) module encodes a task/context embedding into non-negative gains. These gains scale (rotate) a fixed random projection of the shared features before the OWM-trained classifier. As a result, identical inputs get different representations under different contexts.
papers.setting: Supervised: shuffled and disjoint MNIST, disjoint CIFAR-10, ImageNet with a fixed feature extractor, 3,755-class Chinese characters, and 40 CelebA attributes learned one after another on the same face images with a single classifier.
papers.results_vs_baselines: Disjoint CIFAR-10 (end-to-end): 52.83 vs EWC 31.09 and IMM 32.36. About 92% on 3,755 sequentially learned Chinese characters. With CDP, 40 context-dependent tasks on identical face images reach accuracy very close to multi-task training with 40 separate classifiers (about 90%).
papers.relevance: Your conflict states are the 'same stimulus, different response' case that CDP was built for: Pick holds and Stack releases on near-identical observations. CDP shows one network can serve both when a skill context gates the shared features, and OWM keeps the gate and the readout from overwriting each other. For an RSI robot this is a cleaner single-network story than a separate head per skill. The alpha regularizer is the earliest soft version of 'how hard to block old directions'.

papers.citation: Danruo Deng, Guangyong Chen, Jianye Hao, Qiong Wang, Pheng-Ann Heng. Flattening Sharpness for Dynamic Gradient Projection Memory Benefits Continual Learning (FS-DGPM). NeurIPS 2021.
papers.mechanism: Each GPM basis u_i gets a soft importance lambda_i in [0,1], initialized to 1, and the update is (I - M·Lambda·M^T)·grad. lambda_i is learned by gradient descent on the loss of the current batch plus a small replay batch. To first order, dL/dlambda_i is proportional to (g_new·u_i)(u_i·g_joint): a basis where new and old gradients agree is released (lambda falls), and a conflicting one is tightened. A sigmoid with temperature 10 keeps lambda in [0,1]. A sharpness term (adversarial weight perturbation inside the protected subspace) flattens the loss landscape.
papers.setting: Supervised: PMNIST, 10-split CIFAR-100, 20-task CIFAR-100 superclass, 40-task TinyImageNet. Replay buffers of 200-1000 samples; SGD.
papers.results_vs_baselines: CIFAR-100 ACC 74.33 vs GPM 73.18, but BWT -2.71 vs -1.17. Superclass 58.81 vs 57.33 (BWT -2.97 vs -0.37). TinyImageNet 70.41 vs 67.39. According to the SGP paper, it costs about an order of magnitude more training time than GPM.
papers.relevance: The only surveyed method that learns, direction by direction, which of the old skill's directions to open. It uses exactly the signal you measured: alignment of new and old gradients along each basis. In sim, replay of Pick states is free. Your finding that conflict oscillates step to step predicts noisy lambdas under PPO, so this is the place to test smoothing or larger batches. Its higher ACC came with worse BWT than GPM, a warning that learned opening leaks.

papers.citation: Zhen Zhao, Zhizhong Zhang, Xin Tan, Jun Liu, Yanyun Qu, Yuan Xie, Lizhuang Ma. Rethinking Gradient Projection Continual Learning: Stability / Plasticity Feature Space Decoupling. CVPR 2023.
papers.mechanism: Splits the protected feature space into two parts. The intersection subspace I is the sum of intersections between each new task's subspace and the old ones, i.e. directions shared by several tasks. Its residual R holds task-specific directions. R is approximated with a lower energy threshold (eps_R = 0.94 vs eps_I = 0.99), so fewer task-specific directions are frozen. R also gets slightly leakier projection factors (zeta_R = 5e-5 vs zeta_I = 1e-6). The authors back the split with a measurement: a unit update inside I interferes with old tasks far more than one inside R. It works as a plug-in for GPM, TRGP and Adam-NSCL.
papers.setting: Supervised: 10- and 20-split CIFAR-100, 20-split MiniImageNet.
papers.results_vs_baselines: 20-split CIFAR-100 ACC: GPM+SD 80.71 vs GPM 77.53; TRGP+SD 83.84 vs 80.68; Adam-NSCL+SD 76.5 vs 75.81. MiniImageNet: TRGP+SD 65.8 vs 63.51. BWT unchanged or better. Ablation: most of the gain comes from keeping fewer task-specific bases (GPM 77.53 -> 79.99). Leaking through the projections alone helps less and worsens BWT.
papers.relevance: Gives a structural rule for which old directions are safe to open. Directions shared by several skills (likely the reach and grasp primitives in your library) stay frozen, while directions specific to one old skill can be thinned. It only matters once there are 2+ old skills (Pick, Push, Stack experts). So it belongs in the multi-skill RSI sequence of the full paper rather than the 2-skill abstract.

papers.citation: Gobinda Saha, Isha Garg, Kaushik Roy. Gradient Projection Memory for Continual Learning (GPM). ICLR 2021 (oral).
papers.mechanism: After each task, GPM feeds 100-300 samples through the network and takes the SVD of each layer's input representation matrix. It keeps the smallest k bases whose energy reaches eps_th (for example 0.97 plus 0.003 per task on CIFAR-100; 0.95/0.99 on PMNIST). New-task gradients are projected orthogonal to this stored 'core gradient space' (grad - grad·M·M^T). Directions, once stored, are never reopened.
papers.setting: Supervised: PMNIST, 10-split CIFAR-100 (AlexNet), 20-split miniImageNet and 5-Datasets (ResNet-18). Multi-head except PMNIST.
papers.results_vs_baselines: ACC: PMNIST 93.91 vs OWM 90.71, EWC 89.97, A-GEM 83.56, OGD 82.56. CIFAR-100 72.48 vs HAT 72.06, EWC 68.80, OWM 50.94. miniImageNet 60.41 vs HAT 59.78. BWT is about 0-3% forgetting. On 5-Datasets, 78% of the gradient space is already constrained after 5 tasks, and the authors note that new learning stops once it fills.
papers.relevance: occupancy_test.py already computes GPM's memory (99% energy: 10/42 input dims, about 20/256 hidden, 58/256 last). So this baseline costs you almost nothing, and it is the first one reviewers will ask for. Expect it to behave like your output-only arm: with 94-97% of Stack's input energy inside Pick's bases, only roughly 17-25% of each hidden layer's gradient norm survives the projection. Its multi-head task-incremental protocol is the same as your old-head retention eval, so the comparison is like for like.

papers.citation: Shipeng Wang, Xiaorong Li, Jian Sun, Zongben Xu. Training Networks in Null Space of Feature Covariance for Continual Learning (Adam-NSCL). CVPR 2021 (oral).
papers.mechanism: Keeps an incrementally updated, uncentered covariance of all previous inputs at each linear layer. Its approximate null space is the singular vectors with singular value <= a·lambda_min (a = 10-50; the dropped part explains less than about 5% of the covariance). Adam's candidate update for the new task is projected into that null space layer by layer (Delta = U2·U2^T·g_Adam). The paper proves this projected step is still a descent direction. Opening rule: a cutoff relative to the smallest eigenvalue.
papers.setting: Supervised class splits with ResNet-18: 10-split and 20-split CIFAR-100, 25-split TinyImageNet.
papers.results_vs_baselines: 10-split CIFAR-100: 73.77/-1.6 vs OWM 68.89/-1.88; EWC, LwF and GD-WILD reach lower ACC. 20-split: 75.95/-3.66; GD-WILD scores 1.21 higher ACC but uses external data. TinyImageNet: 58.28/-6.05 vs OWM 49.98/-3.64. In later comparisons (TRGP, Space Decoupling) it trails GPM and TRGP on BWT.
papers.relevance: The cleanest formulation of 'train only in directions Pick never excites'. Like SGP's PPO setup, it projects the Adam step rather than the raw gradient. Its a·lambda_min cutoff is an alternative to GPM's energy threshold for deciding how much of the 256-d space Pick 'owns'. Like GPM, it predicts little plasticity for Stack given your overlap.

papers.citation: Yibo Yang et al. CorDA: Context-Oriented Decomposition Adaptation of Large Language Models for Task-Aware Parameter-Efficient Fine-tuning. NeurIPS 2024.
papers.mechanism: In knowledge-preserved mode, 256 samples of the capability to preserve (NQ-open questions) are run through the model, and each linear layer's input covariance C = X·X^T is formed. CorDA takes the SVD of W·C and uses the r = 128 components with the smallest singular values (mapped back through C^{-1}) as the trainable adapter. The principal components, which carry the preserved context, stay frozen. Opening rule: weight directions ranked by how strongly the preserved data drives them.
papers.setting: LLaMA-2-7B fine-tuned on math (MetaMathQA), code and instruction following, while measuring retention of world knowledge (TriviaQA, NQ-open, WebQS).
papers.results_vs_baselines: Math run: NQ-open retention 9.36 vs LoRA 1.91, PiSSA 1.02 and full FT 3.13 (base model 14.99). GSM8k 44.58 vs LoRA 42.68 (full FT 48.90, PiSSA 51.48). Best average of task and knowledge scores in all three settings. Ablation: taking the smallest components of plain SVD (no covariance) keeps only 4.21 NQ, so the data context is what makes the direction choice work.
papers.relevance: Decides which weight directions belong to the old skill by asking which ones the old skill's data actually drives (W·C), not by weight magnitude. The direct analogue is using Pick-state activations to choose Stack's trainable subspace. It shows the usual cost: directions chosen to preserve knowledge learn the new task more slowly (GSM8k below full FT), which matches your partial-training speed gap.

papers.citation: Yan-Shuo Liang, Wu-Jun Li. InfLoRA: Interference-Free Low-Rank Adaptation for Continual Learning. CVPR 2024. (Follow-up: KeepLoRA, ICLR 2026, arXiv:2601.19659.)
papers.mechanism: For each new task, the LoRA down-projection B_t is fixed before training and frozen. Its rows are the top-r singular directions of the new task's layer inputs after removing the old tasks' subspace (maintained by DualGPM, threshold 0.95-0.98 rising over tasks). They therefore lie in the new task's gradient space intersected with the complement of the old space. Only A_t is trained, starting from zero. The paper proves this is equivalent to fine-tuning the pre-trained weight within that subspace. Follow-up KeepLoRA keeps the down-projection orthogonal to both the pre-trained principal subspace and prior-task features, initialized from the gradient projected onto the residual space.
papers.setting: Class-incremental learning with a pre-trained ViT-B/16: ImageNet-R (5/10/20 tasks), CIFAR-100, DomainNet.
papers.results_vs_baselines: ImageNet-R, 10 tasks, final ACC: 75.65 vs CODA-P 71.47, C-LoRA 71.89, LAE 71.70, SeqLoRA 64.32. 20 tasks: 71.01 vs 67.28 (CODA-P). DomainNet: 74.53 vs 73.23. Ablation: restricting B to the old-space complement alone, without aligning it to the new task's gradient space, gives the worst new-task accuracy.
papers.relevance: A recipe for 'train only what the new skill needs': a per-skill low-rank adapter whose input side is the new skill's top directions outside the old skill's space. Your full-FT change is already low rank (10-23 directions per layer), so a rank-16-32 per-skill adapter is the right size. Your overlap is the warning: Stack's top directions mostly lie inside Pick's space, so the part outside it will be thin, the same failure as GPM. Use it as a baseline, not as your method.

papers.citation: Jean-Baptiste Gaya, Thang Doan, Lucas Caccia, Laure Soulier, Ludovic Denoyer, Roberta Raileanu. Building a Subspace of Policies for Scalable Continual Learning (CSP). ICLR 2023 (notable top 25%).
papers.mechanism: Maintains a simplex of policies in parameter space, spanned by anchor networks. For a new task, CSP adds an anchor (old anchors frozen) and trains with convex weights alpha sampled from a Dirichlet distribution. An alpha-conditioned critic finds the best point in the subspace. The new anchor is kept only if the best point in the extended subspace beats the best old point by a factor of 1 + eps, with eps = 0.1. Otherwise the anchor is pruned and the task reuses the old subspace. Each task stores only its alpha, so old tasks are never changed. The reuse-vs-grow decision is empirical and made per task.
papers.setting: Continual RL with SAC: Brax HalfCheetah and Ant (8-task scenarios) and Humanoid; Continual World CW10 (Meta-World manipulation).
papers.results_vs_baselines: Brax performance normalized to one SAC per task. HalfCheetah 1.27 at 5.4 policy-sizes, vs PackNet 0.85, EWC 0.43, FT-1 0.62, SAC-N 1.00 at 8 sizes. Ant 1.11 vs PackNet 1.08. Humanoid 1.76 vs 1.00. Forgetting is about 0, with about 4-5 anchors for 8 tasks. CW10: 0.81 with about 5.3 heads vs PackNet 0.83 (10 heads), EWC 0.66, FT-1 0.10.
papers.relevance: The only subspace-style continual-RL method with manipulation results. It supplies what your PullCube case needs: an explicit task-level test of whether reuse helps (grow only if the old subspace falls short by more than 10%). That turns 'reuse hurts for reversed skills' into a built-in gate rather than a failure case. It works by weight-space interpolation rather than activation subspaces, so it complements GPM-style direction selection.

papers.citation: Xiao Wang et al. Orthogonal Subspace Learning for Language Model Continual Learning (O-LoRA). Findings of EMNLP 2023.
papers.mechanism: Each task gets its own LoRA. Earlier LoRAs are frozen, and the new one is trained with a penalty lambda·sum_i ||A_i^T A_t||^2 (lambda = 0.5). The penalty pushes its input-side subspace to be orthogonal to the earlier adapters', which are assumed to summarize earlier tasks' gradient subspaces. Adapters are merged into the base weights after training. A task ID is needed during training but not at inference.
papers.setting: T5-large on a 4-task text-classification continual-learning benchmark and a 15-task long sequence.
papers.results_vs_baselines: Standard benchmark average 75.8 vs LFPT5 72.7, ProgPrompt 75.1, EWC 50.3, SeqFT 28.5 (multi-task upper bound 80.0). Long sequence 69.6 vs LFPT5 69.2, but below ProgPrompt 77.9 and per-task FT 78.1. In OrthoSkillVLA's robot study, O-LoRA reaches only 30.5% final success rate.
papers.relevance: Mostly a 'do not do this' data point. Orthogonality between adapter parameters ignores where the old skill's data actually lives. Your Pick expert was trained by full RL, so there is no old adapter to be orthogonal to. It becomes relevant only between successively added skill adapters (for example Stack vs Place). Reviewers know it as the standard LoRA continual-learning baseline, and it did badly on robot skills.

takeaways: Prediction for the hard-constraint family (GPM, Adam-NSCL, InfLoRA, NESS from CPAL 2026, AlphaEdit): it should land near your output-only arm (about 3M steps, about 0.99 retention), not near full FT. With 94-97% of Stack's activation energy inside Pick's subspace, only roughly 17-25% of each hidden layer's gradient norm survives the projection. Run GPM anyway: the bases already come out of occupancy_test.py, and its predicted failure is the cleanest motivation for opening directions.

Choose directions, not neurons. Two of your results fit a dense, low-rank footprint: importance-picked units do no better than random units, and the full-FT change is spread over about 190/256 units. Pick lives in about 20 rotated directions mixed into every unit, so any 5% unit subset touches it about equally. XdG (Masse et al., PNAS 2018) found random context-gating of units works for the same reason. Every method surveyed makes the share/unshare decision on singular directions. Cheap check first: the participation ratio of Pick's top singular vectors across units. Then swap --train_units masks for direction masks or per-direction scales.

How the literature decides which old directions to open, and which rules your data allow: (a) Old-task energy: SGP's lambda from sigma, Adam-NSCL's a·lambda_min cutoff, CorDA's W·C ranking, GPM's eps_th. (b) Alignment of new and old gradients: CUBER (layer-wise cosine), FS-DGPM (per-basis gradient product). (c) Relevance to the new task: TRGP's projection ratio; the top new-gradient directions used by InfLoRA, KeepLoRA and OrthoSkillVLA. (d) Position or sharing: OrthoSkillVLA (action head 0.9999 vs backbone 0.99); Space Decoupling (directions shared by several skills kept strict). Your measurements make (c) uninformative, since Pick is relevant in every layer, and (b) noisy from step to step. Start with (a)+(d): SGP-style soft scaling with the strictest setting at the last hidden layer. Use (b) only with EMA smoothing over PPO epochs and a freshly computed retention gradient.

Biggest lever: protect Pick's function, not Pick's representation. Almost every method here freezes all directions the old inputs use. Under your protocol (the old head reading the new trunk), only the old head's 8 action means on Pick states need to stay fixed, and that head ignores 248 of the 256 last-layer directions. OGD (projecting off output gradients) and AlphaEdit (preserving outputs on preserved keys) are the function-space versions. A sim-native variant projects the PPO Adam step off the Jacobian of the old head's action mean on a fresh batch of expert-rollout states. That is at most a few thousand rows for a ~1e5-parameter actor, cheap on a 4090. A KL penalty on the same states is the soft version. One-hour diagnostic before building it: on a batch of Stack PPO gradients, measure the fraction of gradient norm that survives (i) GPM projection and (ii) old-output-Jacobian projection. If (ii) is far above the roughly 20% from (i), this is the method. We found no RL paper doing this, so it is a candidate contribution, not an established result.

Where to unshare. The conflict states (Pick holds, Stack releases) sit on Pick's densest directions, so no shared-weight change can serve both skills on near-identical inputs. The literature resolves this with small private parameters: TRGP/CUBER's k x k scaling matrix inside the old subspace (k = 10 to about 20 for your layers, so roughly 1k parameters per skill), OWM's context-gated features, OrthoSkillVLA's per-skill output experts, and CSP's per-task alpha. Candidate recipe for 'what to share, where to unshare': shared weights move only in function-safe or low-importance directions; Stack gets a private map on Pick's high-energy directions (TRGP-style Q, or an adapter whose input side is fixed to Pick's bases); plus a per-skill head. First find where full FT's speed edge comes from: plot per-stage curves (first release at the goal vs stable placement) for output-only and full FT. If the gap is in the post-release new territory, soft opening is enough; if it is at the conflict states, you need the private map.

Simulation makes old-task data free, which removes the assumption that shaped the GPM family (no replay, so store bases or end-of-training gradients). You can recompute bases, retention gradients and old-output Jacobians every PPO iteration from frozen-expert rollouts, and track retention online. It also makes 'PPO + BC or KL on old-skill states' a mandatory baseline. In Wolczyk et al. (ICML 2024), BC was the most effective retention method on Meta-World RoboticSequence (SAC): all 4 stages solved 80% of the time, while vanilla fine-tuning was no better than training from scratch. A-GEM/PCGrad-style conflict projection against that retention gradient is the other cheap baseline (PCGrad, NeurIPS 2020, was run with SAC on Meta-World). RL's Razor (ICLR 2026) found forgetting is predicted by the KL between the fine-tuned and base policy on the new task's states. So KL-to-Pick on Stack states is a baseline that needs no old data, and KL on Pick states is a cheap per-iteration retention proxy next to retention_eval.py.

Optimizer detail that will bite: with Adam, project the update Adam produces, not the gradient you feed into it. Adam's per-coordinate scaling pushes a projected gradient back out of a rotated subspace. Axis-aligned unit masks survive this, which is likely why --train_units worked, as long as moments start at zero and there is no weight decay. SGP saw catastrophic forgetting in PPO-Atari when projected gradients went into Adam, and fixed it by projecting Adam's output. Adam-NSCL likewise projects Adam's candidate step. Log the weight change inside the protected directions to confirm it stays near zero.

Positioning and baselines. Subspace continual learning is almost untested in on-policy RL: only SGP (PPO, 6 Atari games) and CSP (SAC, Brax and Continual World). OrthoSkillVLA (PRCV 2026) is imitation-only, and none of the three studies stage-extension skills, shared conflict states, or the exploration floor you found decisive. That gap is defensible for RSS. Expected baseline table: full FT, FT + BC/KL, output-only, GPM (hard), SGP (soft), TRGP (private Q), and your method. Report steps to 90% on the new skill and old-skill success through the old head, mirroring the ACC/BWT/FWT used by CUBER and TRGP. Your multi-head retention protocol is exactly their task-incremental protocol, so their baselines drop in unchanged.

Reversed skills need a reuse gate, not a better projection. For PullCube from Push (scratch 1.2M steps vs reuse above 7M or never), every opening rule still ties Pull to Push's representation. Two principled switches exist. CSP's grow-or-reuse test keeps the new anchor only if it beats the best old point by 10%. CUBER's regimes say: strong overlap with negative correlation means protect the old skill and reuse only through private parameters. Practical version: a short probe run of 'reuse' vs 'fresh private branch', keeping whichever is faster. Presented as part of the method, this turns the negative result into a feature.

Scaling to the RSI sequence for the full paper. Hard-projection capacity runs out: GPM had 78% of the gradient space constrained after 5 dissimilar tasks. SGP (only 18-37% of stored directions fully blocked after 20 tasks) and E2-LoRA (ICML 2026) argue for importance-weighted, energy-compacted memories. E2-LoRA's basis is that output drift dW·X is low rank, so it keeps each task's leading directions and releases the rest. Your full-FT update is also low rank (10-23 directions per layer). Measure how many new directions each added skill actually claims per layer. If it is about 20, a 256-wide layer saturates after roughly 10 skills, a concrete scaling claim to test on a Pick -> Stack -> Place -> ... chain.

papers.citation: Wołczyk, Zając, Pascanu, Kuciński, Miłoś. Continual World: A Robotic Benchmark For Continual Reinforcement Learning. NeurIPS 2021.
papers.mechanism: This is a benchmark and protocol, not a method. It defines the continual-RL metrics most later robot RL papers reuse. Average success P(T). Forgetting F_i = p_i(end of task i) − p_i(T). Forward transfer FT_i = (AUC_i − AUC_i^ref)/(1 − AUC_i^ref), measured against a from-scratch single-task reference curve. Reference transfer RT is the mean, over tasks, of the best single-source fine-tune transfer from a 10×10 transfer matrix, i.e. what a CL method should at least match. The actor and critic have one head per task, so task id is used at test. Only the actor is regularized. 20 seeds with 90% bootstrap CIs.
papers.setting: Meta-World Sawyer arm, 12-D state, 4-D action. CW10 is 10 tasks × 1M SAC steps; CW20 is CW10 run twice; 3-task triplets are provided for fast iteration. 4×256 MLP. Compares 7 CL methods (L2, EWC, MAS, VCL, PackNet, Perfect Memory/reservoir, A-GEM), fine-tuning and multitask.
papers.results_vs_baselines: CW20 performance / forgetting / FT: PackNet 0.80/0.00/0.19; EWC 0.60/0.02/−0.17; MAS 0.51/0.00/−0.52; VCL 0.48/0.01/−0.49; L2 0.43/0.02/−0.71; fine-tuning 0.05/0.73/0.20; A-GEM 0.07/0.71/0.13; Perfect Memory 0.12/0.07/−1.34. Multitask 0.51 (0.65 with PopArt). RT = 0.46. Only fine-tuning and PackNet get positive FT. PackNet needs task id at evaluation, +50% params, +15% time, and a capacity split fixed in advance.
papers.relevance: These are the metric definitions reviewers expect. Map our steps-to-90% onto FT against a scratch reference, and report RT so that 'reuse' is judged against simply fine-tuning from the best earlier skill. The benchmark shows the same trade-off we measured: regularizers stop forgetting but also stop transfer, while fine-tuning transfers but forgets. PackNet is the direct competitor to training a unit subset in place, because it keeps one network and forgets nothing by construction. Their 20-seed standard is far above our 2-6 seeds.

papers.citation: Kim, Lee, Narang, Guo. ACCRUE: Continual Off-Policy Reinforcement Learning for Robot Foundation Models. arXiv 2610.18596, Oct 2026 (NVIDIA/KAIST; no venue yet).
papers.mechanism: A lightweight actor and critic sit on frozen DINOv3 features and are conditioned on the base VLA's reference action chunk. Both are carried from stage to stage. The critic trains only on current-task transitions. The actor loss is current-task RL plus distillation toward cached outputs of the previous-stage actor on a bounded memory of the last 20-100 episodes per earlier task. Task identity, given as the language instruction, is known at test.
papers.setting: Isaac Lab FORGE: peg insert, gear mesh and nut thread as 3-stage sequences in 4 orderings. AutoMate: four 5-stage plug-insertion sequences. 4 seeds per order; FastSAC, 64 envs, 500K steps per stage. Real DROID: a 3-stage NIST board sequence and a 5-stage AutoMate sequence with a π0.5 base and FastTD3, 20 trials per earlier task. Metrics: FWT, NBT, continual AUC, final accuracy, final forgetting, and real-robot RL time.
papers.results_vs_baselines: FORGE, NBT / FWT / AUC / final accuracy / final forgetting: ACCRUE 0.065/0.823/0.869/0.917/0.068; Sequential 0.427/0.819/0.718/0.685/0.409; EWC 0.217/0.593/0.582/0.603/0.224; RETAIN 0.514/0.802/0.682/0.644/0.474; ER 0.518/0.833/0.697/0.626/0.516. Simple Recipe has the lowest NBT (0.038) but FWT only 0.586. Isolated (one learner per task) gets FWT 0.816, AUC 0.868, accuracy 0.919, and ACCRUE matches it with one shared actor-critic. AutoMate: ACCRUE NBT 0.047, AUC 0.858 vs ER 0.167/0.799. Real robot: 31.0-68.5% less RL time than single-task RL, and every earlier task succeeded on at least 18/20 trials (mean 19.4).
papers.relevance: This is the closest competitor to the a2r insert→insert+turn stage: same simulator family and contact-rich insertion, though off-policy rather than PPO. It is also the clearest template of what RSS/CoRL 2027 reviewers will compare against: multi-stage sequences, 4 orders × 4 seeds, FWT/NBT/AUC/accuracy/forgetting, real-robot time-to-success, 20 trials per earlier task, and a baseline suite of Sequential, EWC, RETAIN, ER, Isolated and single-task RL. Its framing, one shared learner that matches the one-copy-per-task Isolated reference, is exactly the bar our same-network claim has to clear. With PPO, the equivalent of its bounded-replay distillation is a stored old-state buffer plus a KL term.

papers.citation: van de Ven, Tuytelaars, Tolias. Three types of incremental learning. Nature Machine Intelligence 4:1185-1197, 2022.
papers.mechanism: Defines three scenarios. Task-incremental: task identity is available at test, so task-specific components such as heads are allowed. Domain-incremental: the output space stays the same and context is neither given nor needed. Class-incremental: the model must infer context. Argues that results are only comparable within a declared scenario, and that in task-incremental learning the proper lower bound is a separate network per task.
papers.setting: Split MNIST and Split CIFAR-100 under all three scenarios. Methods: EWC, SI, LwF, FROMP, ER, A-GEM, DGR, BI-R, iCaRL, XdG, separate networks.
papers.results_vs_baselines: EWC on Split MNIST scores 99.06% task-incremental, 63.03% domain-incremental and 20.64% class-incremental, against a 19.89% lower bound. Separate networks reach 99.57% task-incremental. Replay (e.g. BI-R 99.61/97.26/94.41) is the only family that does well in all three scenarios. Context-specific components only apply to the task-incremental case.
papers.relevance: Our retention test, PickCube through the new trunk with the OLD output layer, is task-incremental: choosing the head is the task id. In that scenario forgetting can be prevented by design, and the honest baseline is to keep the old expert and fine-tune a copy. That gives 1.5M steps and 0.992 retention at +100% actor parameters, which beats our 5%/20%-unit runs (2.2M/1.75M steps, 0.96-0.99) on both axes. So the paper has to win on parameter growth or single-network deployment. The single shared head result (PickCube 0.72-0.96 after Stack) is a different, harder scenario and needs its own baselines, where replay is typically required.

papers.citation: Wołczyk, Cupiał, Ostaszewski, Bortkiewicz, Zając, Pascanu, Kuciński, Miłoś. Fine-tuning Reinforcement Learning Models is Secretly a Forgetting Mitigation Problem. ICML 2024 (spotlight).
papers.mechanism: Identifies forgetting of pre-trained capabilities. Fine-tuning learns the states it visits early (CLOSE) and meanwhile destroys pre-trained behaviour on states it only reaches later (FAR); the paper calls these the state-coverage gap and the imperfect-cloning gap. Tested fixes: EWC; BC replay (KL(π*||π) on stored states labelled by the pre-trained policy); kickstarting (the same KL on current on-policy states); and episodic memory. Retention is applied to the actor only, not the critic.
papers.setting: RoboticSequence: Meta-World hammer→push→peg-unplug-side→push-wall within one episode, with π* pre-trained on the last two stages, trained with SAC. Also Montezuma's Revenge (PPO+RND) and NetHack (APPO).
papers.results_vs_baselines: RoboticSequence: vanilla fine-tuning is about the same as training from scratch. BC is best and solves all four stages about 80% of the time, followed by episodic memory and then EWC. Per-stage curves show FAR-stage success collapsing early under vanilla fine-tuning. NetHack Human Monk: score rises from about 5K to over 10K with retention. EWC always beats vanilla fine-tuning but trails BC, kickstarting and episodic memory.
papers.relevance: This is the canonical reference for stage-structured skills such as our Pick→Stack and Push→PushRetreat pairs. It also supplies the cheapest strong baselines: kickstarting (KL to the old policy on new-task states, no stored data; our --prior_ckpt/--copy_loss without the gate) and BC replay (KL on a small stored set of old-skill states). Reviewers will expect per-stage success curves (reach, grasp, lift, place, release) that show where forgetting happens.

papers.citation: Wołczyk, Zając, Pascanu, Kuciński, Miłoś. Disentangling Transfer in Continual Reinforcement Learning (ClonEx-SAC). NeurIPS 2022.
papers.mechanism: Decomposes transfer into actor, critic, exploration and data. The resulting recipe, ClonEx-SAC: behavioural cloning of past actors on a small stored buffer (actor-only KL), plus exploration at the start of each new task by the best previous policy instead of uniform random actions. The critic is not regularized.
papers.setting: Continual World. The two-task analysis covers all 100 CW10 task pairs; the full runs use CW10 and CW20. SAC, multi-head and single-head, 10 seeds, 90% bootstrap CIs.
papers.results_vs_baselines: Final CW success 87% vs PackNet's 80%, and the CW transfer metric rises from 0.18 to 0.54. BC rehearsal on CW10 (performance/FT): 0.84/0.41, vs PackNet 0.84/0.26, Perfect Memory 0.27/−1.13, fine-tuning 0.10/0.31; on CW20 0.83/0.36 vs PackNet 0.80/0.18. Exploring with previous policies raises EWC's CW10 FT from 0.03 to 0.24-0.25. In the two-task setting, carrying over the critic gives FT 0.20, vs 0.06 for the actor and 0.09 for exploration. Training only the critic's head on a frozen critic body gives FT −1.29, negative on all 100 pairs.
papers.relevance: It reported two of our findings first: exploration is a main transfer lever, and constraining the wrong part of the network hurts. Controls we need: give every baseline the same gripper exploration floor, or exploration gains get credited to reuse. Report critic treatment: our --freeze_trunk freezes only the actor's hidden layers, which is fine, but --init_actor_only re-initializes the critic, the component this paper finds carries the most transfer. And BC on old-skill states (actor only) is the replay baseline to beat.

papers.citation: Du, Sun, Xu, Shah, Itkina, Song. Memory Anchors for Continual Robot Learning. arXiv 2608.26545, Aug 2026.
papers.mechanism: Shows that forgetting is driven by a small set of old-task samples, the 'anchors'. They lie where new-task observations collapse onto old-task representations in the policy latent while the two tasks need conflicting actions. Anchors are found in three steps: latent-overlap clustering, an action-disagreement filter (denoising disagreement above μ+2σ), and kNN retrieval. AnchorER enriches the replay buffer with them.
papers.setting: Behaviour cloning with a U-Net diffusion policy and ResNet-18 encoder on LIBERO Long/Goal/Object/Spatial (10 tasks each, 3 permutations, 1000-memory buffer); also π0.5 with full fine-tuning. Real ARX arm: OpenJar (three similar-looking jars with conflicting opening strategies) and bimanual SweaterFold, 20 rollouts per condition.
papers.results_vs_baselines: Dropping 10% of anchors from the buffer raises forgetting more than 4.5×. Anchor replay cuts forgetting on high-conflict task pairs by more than 63%. LIBERO-Goal NBT: 0.11 vs MIR 0.14, GSS 0.17, random ER 0.18. π0.5 with a 1% buffer: NBT 0.35 vs 0.45. Real robot: 1.7× higher success than random replay. The authors note their sequences are only 3-10 tasks.
papers.relevance: This is nearly our diagnosis: the Pick-hold vs Stack-release conflict states sit in the densest part of the old skill's representation. It appeared two months ago, so our representation findings are confirmatory, not novel. Our contribution has to be a parameter-level, replay-free recipe. Reviewers will ask for the matched sample-level baseline: store the old expert's actions at the done-probe/conflict states (a tiny anchor buffer) and distill there. It also defines a task-conflict NBT metric for conflicting pairs.

papers.citation: Liu, Zhang, Asadi, Liu, Zhao, Sabach, Fakoor. TAIL: Task-specific Adapters for Imitation Learning with Large Pretrained Models. ICLR 2024.
