papers.mechanism: Freezes the pretrained policy and adds one parameter-efficient adapter per task (LoRA, bottleneck/RoboAdapter, or prefix). The adapter is chosen by task id at test, and old adapters are never touched, so forgetting is zero by construction.
papers.setting: Pretrained on 40 LIBERO-90 kitchen tasks, then adapted in sequence to the Spatial, Goal, Object, Living Room and Study Room suites (8 tasks each), and separately to LIBERO-10. Imitation learning, 3 seeds. Baselines: full fine-tuning, frozen pretrained features, ER, EWC, PackNet.
papers.results_vs_baselines: LIBERO-10 FWT/BWT: LoRA 0.70/0 vs full fine-tuning 0.48/−0.55, ER 0.45/−0.49, EWC 0.30/−0.43. LoRA trains 1.17% of parameters (2.0M of 172M) and uses 23% less GPU memory. Full fine-tuning lost 0.15-0.26 success on revisited suites even when retrained on the same data. A LoRA adapter takes 7.8 MB, vs about 28 GB for replay data.
papers.relevance: With task id available, as in our multi-head setup, a per-skill LoRA on the frozen trunk forgets nothing, adds about 1-5% parameters, and here transferred better than full fine-tuning. It competes directly with training 5-20% of units in place, which forgets 1-3 points. It must appear in our tables, with a rank sweep on the MLP and later on the a2r residual trunk. Our method has to beat it on steps-to-90%, or on something adapters cannot do, such as working without task id or composing skills.

papers.citation: Liu, Zhu, Gao, Feng, Liu, Zhu, Stone. LIBERO: Benchmarking Knowledge Transfer for Lifelong Robot Learning. NeurIPS 2023 Datasets & Benchmarks.
papers.mechanism: Benchmark and protocol for lifelong decision making. FWT is mean success while training on each new task; NBT is the mean drop of each task from its best to later stages; AUC combines the two. All are computed from a success matrix with best-checkpoint selection. Also studies architectures, algorithms, task ordering (5 orders), language vs task-ID embeddings, and pretraining.
papers.setting: 130 language-conditioned manipulation tasks: Spatial, Object, Goal and Long suites of 10, plus LIBERO-90 for pretraining. 50 demos per task, behaviour cloning, 3 seeds. Baselines: sequential fine-tuning (SEQL), ER, EWC, PackNet, multitask.
papers.results_vs_baselines: LIBERO-Long FWT/NBT/AUC: SEQL 0.54/0.63/0.15, ER 0.48/0.32/0.32, EWC 0.13/0.22/0.02, PackNet 0.22/0.08/0.25; multitask AUC 0.48. PackNet has the best AUC on Spatial and Goal (0.63/0.75). Sequential fine-tuning has the best FWT on every suite, and ER is the most robust. Task order changes results significantly, especially for PackNet. Task-ID and language embeddings perform the same. Naive pretraining on LIBERO-90 hurt.
papers.relevance: FWT/NBT/AUC is the vocabulary RSS/CoRL reviewers now use (ACCRUE, Memory Anchors and the RSS 2026 LifeLong-RFT paper all report it), so report it alongside the CW metrics. The order study is why reviewers ask for 2-3 or more orders. PackNet's capacity split hurting FWT on long tasks predicts the cost of training only 5-20% of units; show where that breaks as skills accumulate.

papers.citation: Yadav, Zhou, Wagenmaker, Pertsch, Levine. Robust Finetuning of Vision-Language-Action Robot Policies via Parameter Merging (RETAIN). ICLR 2026.
papers.mechanism: Fine-tune a generalist policy on the new skill, then linearly interpolate the weights: θ = (1−α)θ_pre + α·θ_ft, optionally with separate α per module (vision, language, action expert). A sequential rule merges successive skills into one policy.
papers.setting: Real DROID Franka with π0-FAST-DROID: whiteboard wiping (~50 demos) and plates into a rack (~100 demos). LIBERO-10 tasks with π0. Evaluates the new task in- and out-of-distribution plus retained generalist tasks. Baselines: task fine-tuning, co-fine-tuning, LoRA, frozen-language fine-tuning, scratch.
papers.results_vs_baselines: On DROID, baselines reach 70-80% in-distribution but only 30-50% out-of-distribution. RETAIN reaches over 60% out-of-distribution on plates and about 80% on whiteboard, about 40% higher real success on average than the best prior fine-tuning method, and keeps generalist skills. In the sequential plates→whiteboard run it keeps plates better than co-fine-tuning. Under continual RL elsewhere it is weaker: FORGE NBT 0.514 in ACCRUE; LIBERO-Spatial AVG 66.0 vs 81.2 in Simple Recipe.
papers.relevance: A one-line, post-hoc baseline that can be run from our existing checkpoints. Interpolate the full-fine-tuned trunk (1.5M steps, 0.82-0.86 PickCube) with the Pick expert over an α sweep. If some α gives at least 0.97 PickCube while Stack stays at or above 90%, the unit-subset method has no edge. It belongs in the Pareto plot. Note it was accepted at ICLR with only two sequential skills; RSS will want more.

papers.citation: Kessler, Parker-Holder, Ball, Zohren, Roberts. Same State, Different Task: Continual Reinforcement Learning without Interference (OWL). AAAI 2022.
papers.mechanism: Separates interference (the same observation needs different actions in different tasks) from forgetting. OWL uses a shared feature trunk regularized with EWC plus one policy/Q head per task. At test time it picks the head with an exponential-weights multi-armed bandit on TD or reward-likelihood feedback, so no task id is needed.
papers.setting: Pendulum with goals at +90° vs −90° (SAC), and five MiniGrid tasks with near-identical observations (DQN). 10 seeds, median and IQR.
papers.results_vs_baselines: In Pendulum, a single-predictor agent with shared replay settles at a 0° compromise that is wrong for both tasks. MiniGrid SimpleCrossing: experience replay 0.01; OWL with a task oracle 0.85; OWL with the bandit 0.59. Full rehearsal (a buffer and head per task) reaches 0.99 as an upper bound. Removing EWC from the trunk drops OWL to 0.40-0.50.
papers.relevance: Pick (hold at the goal) vs Stack (release at the goal) is exactly this same-state, different-task case: one head seeing identical inputs cannot be right for both. So the paper must say how the skill is chosen at test time: a head index or skill command, or a learned selector such as OWL's bandit or our done-probe. The single-head result should be read as interference, not forgetting. 'Shared trunk + per-skill head + trunk regularizer' is also a baseline very close to our setup.

papers.citation: Malagón, Ceberio, Lozano. Self-Composing Policies for Scalable Continual Reinforcement Learning (CompoNet). ICML 2024 (oral).
papers.mechanism: A growing modular policy: one new module per task, with earlier modules frozen. Each module attends over the outputs of the earlier modules' policies plus its own internal policy, so no separate composer network is needed. Parameters grow linearly with the number of tasks; there is no forgetting and no capacity loss.
papers.setting: Meta-World CW20 sequence (SAC, v2 tasks, 1M steps per task); ALE SpaceInvaders (10 modes) and Freeway (7 modes) with PPO. 10 seeds. Reports performance, CW-style forward transfer, RT, and memory and inference cost against the number of tasks.
papers.results_vs_baselines: Meta-World performance/FT: CompoNet 0.42/0.01, ProgressiveNet 0.41/−0.04, PackNet 0.24/−0.67, FT-N (a fine-tuned copy kept per task) 0.37/−0.21, FT-1 (one network fine-tuned throughout) 0.03/−0.21, scratch 0.06; RT −0.06. CompoNet is the only method with positive FT there. Freeway: 0.94/0.80 vs FT-N 0.81/0.64. SpaceInvaders: ties FT-N at 0.99. Inference cost grows more slowly than ProgressiveNet's.
papers.relevance: Supplies the growth-family baselines (FT-N, ProgressiveNet, PackNet) and the reporting reviewers expect for parameter growth: parameters per added skill and inference cost against the number of skills, with 10 seeds. FT-N is the strong copy-per-skill reference that our same-network method has to approach while growing much less.

papers.citation: Hu, Shim, Tang, Sung, Liu, Stone, Martín-Martín. Simple Recipe Works: Vision-Language-Action Models are Natural Continual Learners with Reinforcement Learning. RLC 2026 (Reinforcement Learning Journal).
papers.mechanism: Plain sequential fine-tuning of a large pretrained VLA with LoRA (rank 32) and on-policy RL (GRPO). The authors argue the three ingredients together keep updates small and largely in the null space of old tasks; removing any one of them causes forgetting.
papers.setting: OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO-Spatial/Object/Long, plus a 30-task sequence and 3 task re-orders; Pi-0 on RoboCasa; OpenVLA on ManiSkill. 3 seeds. Metrics: AVG, NBT, FWT and zero-shot success (ZS) on held-out tasks. Baselines: EWC, expert replay, DER, dynamic weight expansion, SLCA, RETAIN, multitask oracle.
papers.results_vs_baselines: LIBERO-Spatial AVG/NBT: sequential fine-tuning 81.2/0.3; EWC 66.1/0.7; ER 80.2/0.6; DER 73.4/4.7; weight expansion 79.6/0.0; SLCA 69.9/−0.6; RETAIN 66.0/2.9; multitask 85.8. NBT stays under 2% across settings. Ablations: SFT instead of RL 29.9/78.7; a 12M-parameter policy 13.1/11.4; full fine-tuning without LoRA 7.3/40.9.
papers.relevance: Reviewers may say sequential LoRA plus on-policy RL already forgets little. The paper's own ablations show that small policies and full-parameter updates do forget, which matches our 14-23-point loss from full fine-tuning on a small MLP. That defence only holds if we run a LoRA-on-MLP RL baseline ourselves. Its baseline set and the zero-shot metric on held-out skills are a good template, and it is an RL-venue paper that uses ManiSkill.

papers.citation: Liu, Kim, Liu, Liu, Zhu. Pretrained Vision-Language-Action Models are Surprisingly Resistant to Forgetting in Continual Learning. ICML 2026 (oral).
papers.mechanism: Empirical study comparing pretrained VLAs with from-scratch BC policies under sequential learning, with and without experience replay. Introduces normalized NBT and recovery efficiency (fine-tuning steps needed to regain peak success, as a fraction of the original training). Uses a component-swapping test to locate forgetting: pair the backbone from after task k+1 with the head from task k, and the reverse.
papers.setting: LIBERO Spatial/Object/Goal/10 (10 tasks each, fixed order). Pi0 and GR00T N1.5 (3B) vs BC-Transformer, BC-ViT and diffusion policy (15-26M). Replay buffers of 10, 100 or 1000 samples per task.
papers.results_vs_baselines: With 1000-sample replay: Pi0 SR 0.768 / NBT −0.016 and GR00T 0.919/0.027, vs BC-Diffusion 0.696/0.127 and BC-Transformer 0.585/0.245. LIBERO-10 Pi0 NBT: sequential 0.562, EWC 0.543, ER −0.070. Pi0 recovers forgotten tasks in 6-11% of the original steps, vs 33-187% for BC-Transformer. The vision-language backbone is the main locus of forgetting. A from-scratch Pi0 forgot little only because it learned little.
papers.relevance: Our retention test (old head through the new hidden layers) is this paper's component-swap diagnostic, so cite it to legitimize the protocol, but also report how the deployed policy does. It adds recovery efficiency as a cheap metric for 'damaged but recoverable'. It warns that low forgetting can mean low plasticity, so every retention number should be paired with new-skill steps-to-90%. And it shows that ER with tiny buffers is a baseline reviewers will expect.

papers.citation: Dohare, Hernandez-Garcia, Lan, Rahman, Mahmood, Sutton. Loss of plasticity in deep continual learning. Nature 632:768-774, 2024.
papers.mechanism: Shows that standard backprop gradually loses the ability to learn over long task sequences, tracked by a rising fraction of dead units, growing weight magnitude and falling effective rank of the hidden representation. Continual backpropagation re-initializes a small fraction of low-utility units to keep plasticity; L2 and shrink-and-perturb also help.
papers.setting: Continual ImageNet (thousands of binary tasks), class-incremental CIFAR-100, and Slippery Ant (PPO with ground friction changing over time).
papers.results_vs_baselines: Standard deep networks eventually learn no better than a shallow network on continual ImageNet. Standard PPO fails catastrophically on Slippery Ant, while PPO with L2 or continual backprop keeps performing. In the preprint, up to 25% of units die after 800 Permuted-MNIST tasks.
papers.relevance: A 'keep adding skills' (RSI) claim invites the plasticity question: is skill k still learned as fast as skill 2? Report steps-to-90% on a fixed probe skill after each addition, against scratch, plus the trunk's effective rank and dead-unit fraction. Our measurement that the old skill uses only about 20 of 256 hidden directions suggests spare capacity, but that needs testing over a chain. Continual-backprop-style reset of low-utility units is also a candidate mechanism for 'unsharing'.

papers.citation: Agarwal, Schwarzer, Castro, Courville, Bellemare. Deep Reinforcement Learning at the Edge of the Statistical Precipice. NeurIPS 2021 (outstanding paper).
papers.mechanism: A statistical protocol for RL with few runs: interval estimates from stratified bootstrap CIs, performance profiles, interquartile mean (IQM), optimality gap and probability of improvement. Released as the rliable library.
papers.setting: Re-analysis of published Atari 100k, ALE, Procgen and DMC results.
papers.results_vs_baselines: In the Atari 100k case study, conclusions drawn from point estimates often differed substantially from those drawn from interval estimates. IQM is more robust than the mean and more statistically efficient than the median when runs are few.
papers.relevance: With 2-6 seeds we cannot separate 0.97 from 0.99 retention, or 1.75M from 2.2M steps. Report IQM with 95% stratified bootstrap CIs and the probability of improvement over the strongest baseline. For reference, CW used 20 seeds, CompoNet 10, and ACCRUE 4 seeds × 4 orders.

takeaways: Under task id, a 'same network' only wins on parameters. Our retention test (old output layer on the new trunk) is task-incremental, and there the honest reference is keeping the old expert frozen and fully fine-tuning a copy for the new skill (FT-N / ACCRUE's 'Isolated'). That gets 1.5M steps and 0.992 PickCube at +100% actor parameters, which beats our 5% and 20% unit runs (2.2M and 1.75M steps, 0.96-0.99) on both axes. A per-skill LoRA on the frozen trunk (TAIL) forgets nothing at about 1% parameters, and PackNet forgets nothing with no growth. So the headline has to be a Pareto claim over three things: new-skill steps-to-90%, old-skill retention, and parameters added per skill. The target is to approach Isolated with one network, as ACCRUE does (FWT 0.823 vs 0.816, accuracy 0.917 vs 0.919). If we cannot beat LoRA and PackNet on that frontier, reframe around what they cannot do: no task id at test, one deployable policy, composing skills.

State the scenario and how a skill is selected at test time. Pick-hold vs Stack-release is same-state, different-task interference (OWL), so a single head without a task signal must compromise. Report two results separately: (a) multi-head, with the skill command as task id, which RSS/CoRL accept (LIBERO, ACCRUE and Simple Recipe all give the instruction); and (b) the single-head result (PickCube 0.72-0.96 after Stack) as a harder, task-agnostic case, ideally with a selector such as an OWL-style bandit or our done-probe.

State what old-skill information the method uses during new-skill training. The options, from least to most: weights only (our current runs); teacher queries on new-task states (kickstarting/LwF, which our --prior_ckpt/--copy_loss already supports without the gate); a small stored buffer of old-skill states (BC replay as in ClonEx; ACCRUE keeps 20-100 episodes per task); or rollouts in the old skill's simulator (multitask). 'Replay-free' is a selling point only if we match BC replay and Memory-Anchors-style replay at equal memory, or show we add to them. The anchor-style version is to store the old expert's actions at the done-probe/conflict states.

Minimum baseline table, all with the same gripper exploration floor (ClonEx: exploration alone moved EWC's CW10 transfer from 0.03 to 0.24): scratch; sequential full fine-tuning; head-only (frozen trunk); LP-FT (train the head first, then full fine-tuning; Kumar et al., ICLR 2022, report 10-100× smaller feature change); EWC or L2 on the actor only; kickstarting; BC replay; weight interpolation of the full-FT trunk with the Pick expert (RETAIN α sweep, free from existing checkpoints); per-skill LoRA with a rank sweep; PackNet; FT-N/Isolated; multitask joint training as the oracle and as the interleaved recipe we want to replace; and the random-unit control.

Metrics. Build a success matrix s[j,k], the success on skill k after adding skill j, with at least 1k evaluation episodes per cell (cheap in GPU sim). From it report: final average success; forgetting/NBT, plus task-conflict NBT for conflicting pairs; FWT both as CW's AUC normalized against scratch and as the steps-to-90% ratio against scratch; LIBERO/ACCRUE AUC; CW's reference transfer RT (best single-source fine-tune); parameters added per skill; environment steps and wall-clock. Diagnostics: KL between the new and old policy on new-skill states (RL's Razor, ICLR 2026, finds this predicts forgetting); recovery efficiency; per-stage success (reach, grasp, lift, place, release). Always pair retention with new-skill speed, because low forgetting can just mean low plasticity: in ACCRUE's table Simple Recipe has the lowest NBT (0.038) but FWT only 0.586.

Number of skills, orders and seeds. One pair is a case study. The current bar: ACCRUE uses 3- and 5-stage sequences × 4 orders × 4 seeds; Memory Anchors 10 tasks × 3 permutations; LIBERO 10-task suites with significant order effects; CW 10-20 tasks with 20 seeds. For the April 2027 full paper: at least 4 additions into one ManiSkill network, mixing stage extensions (Pick→Stack, Pick→PlaceCube, Push→PushRetreat at 6 and 10 cm), one unrelated skill and the reversed PullCube; 2-3 orders; 5-10 seeds with rliable IQM and 95% CIs. Then a2r insert→insert+turn reported with ACCRUE's metrics, and on the Piper X, 20 trials of every earlier skill after each addition (ACCRUE and the RSS 2026 LifeLong-RFT paper both used 20 real trials per task).

For the Dec 4 extended abstract: two pairs (Pick→Stack, Push→PushRetreat), 10 seeds, a Pareto plot against FT-N, RETAIN interpolation, kickstarting, BC replay, per-skill LoRA and PackNet, and a clear statement of the scenario. Run RETAIN interpolation and kickstarting first: they are the cheapest experiments that could erase the current advantage.

Critic control. CW, ClonEx and ACCRUE regularize only the actor and let the critic adapt. ClonEx found carrying the critic over is the largest single transfer component (FT 0.20 vs 0.06 for the actor), and a critic trained only at its head was catastrophic (FT −1.29). Our --freeze_trunk freezes only the actor's hidden layers, which is fine, but --init_actor_only re-initializes the critic. Test carrying the critic over (with --critic_warmup) and report the value-network treatment in every row.

Novelty positioning. Three papers already contain our diagnosis: OWL (same-state interference, 2022); Fine-tuning RL is Secretly a Forgetting Mitigation Problem (stage-structured forgetting fixed by BC and kickstarting, ICML 2024); and Memory Anchors (forgetting concentrates where new-task states collapse onto old representations with conflicting actions, Aug 2026). Present our representation results as motivation. The contribution must be a replay-free, parameter-level recipe (where to unshare, which parameters to train) with a better frontier than those baselines. Keep the negative results (choosing units by conflict or importance is no better than random; conflict-local exploration is no better than global), since reviewers will run those controls anyway.

Handle negative transfer rather than hide it. PullCube from the Push expert (scratch 1.2M steps; reuse over 7M or never) is CW's negative-RT case. CompoNet shows a modular method can fall back to learning from scratch when earlier skills don't help. Reset & Distill (arXiv 2403.05066) resets the actor-critic for the new task and then distills the new and old experts into one network. Add a sharing detector or a reset-and-distill fallback, and report RT so readers can see when reuse should not happen.

Plasticity across a chain. After each addition, measure steps-to-90% on a fixed probe skill against scratch, plus the trunk's effective rank and dead-unit fraction (Dohare et al., Nature 2024). The old skill using only about 20 of 256 hidden directions suggests spare capacity, but that is a claim to test, not assume. Resetting low-utility units, as in continual backprop, is a candidate 'unshare' mechanism.

Statistics. Retention gaps of 1-3 points need at least 10 seeds per headline cell and 1k+ evaluation episodes. Report IQM, 95% stratified bootstrap CIs and the probability of improvement over the best baseline (rliable). For comparison: CW used 20 seeds with 90% CIs, CompoNet 10 seeds, LIBERO only 3.

methods.name: FN-PPO: project every Adam step onto the null space of the old skills' outputs (zero growth)
methods.idea: All trunk parameters stay shared with the new skill. What gets protected is only what the old skills actually use: the action means that their own frozen heads produce on their own states. Each PPO iteration rebuilds, on fresh old-skill states, the exact Jacobian rows of those means with respect to the shared trunk, and each Adam step is projected onto the null space of those rows. The part of a step that would change an old skill's behaviour is removed; this is the conflict, and it lives in the shared parameters. Everything else stays shared and trainable, including using the old features as inputs to new features. A Gauss-Newton restore step cancels second-order drift, and the projection multipliers show which old states the new skill would have damaged (a conflict map, at no extra cost). Each skill adds one 8x256 head, a log-std and a critic: 2,064 actor parameters, 1.4% of the 144,656-parameter actor. This is the strongest form of the user's idea: one network, no private trunk parameters.
methods.algorithm:
Notation. Shared trunk θ = {W_l, b_l}, l = 1..3, with h_l = tanh(W_l z_{l-1} + b_l), z_0 = x (42-d), z_1 = h_1, z_2 = h_2. Each skill s has a private head μ_s(x) = W_o^s h_3 + b_o^s (8 outputs), a private log-std and a private critic. When skill k is added, its head starts as a copy of the source head and every earlier head j < k is frozen. The snapshot θ_0 taken at the start of skill k gives the targets μ_j*(x). σ_j is skill j's std.

Once per PPO iteration, after the rollout:
(1) Anchors: N = 512 states per old skill.
- bank: drawn from that skill's stored states. For PickCube this is data/bc_pick_c1.pt, 39,647 expert states with an episode id and a keep mask. Draws are stratified by phase, read from the observation: approach, holding away, holding within 2.5 cm of the goal, released (grasp flag x[18] and |x[39:42]|). Banks are used because ManiSkill's GPU sim cannot host a second task inside the training process. A new skill's bank is collected by a separate call after it finishes, as conflict_concentration.py --collect does.
- self (variant that needs no old data): drawn from the current b_obs.
- Draws use a dedicated torch.Generator, so action noise is unchanged.
(2) Run the current trunk forward on the anchors and keep z_{l-1} and D_l = 1 - h_l^2.
(3) Analytic backprop vectors for every anchor n and action dim a: g_3 = D_3 ⊙ W_o^j[a,:]/σ_{j,a}, g_2 = D_2 ⊙ (W_3^T g_3), g_1 = D_1 ⊙ (W_2^T g_2). Stack them into G_l ∈ R^{M×256} and Z_l ∈ R^{M×in_l}, with M = 8·N·(k-1) (4,096 for one old skill).
(4) Gram matrix of the full trunk Jacobian, without materialising the Jacobian (each row's layer block is the rank-1 matrix g z^T): K = Σ_l (G_l G_l^T) ⊙ (Z_l Z_l^T + 1) + δI, with δ = 1e-4·tr(K)/M. Factor it with Cholesky.

Every Adam step (256 per iteration on Stack: 8 epochs × 32 minibatches):
(5) Backward pass, gradient clip, save θ_prev, optimizer.step(). This gives Adam's trunk step Δ_l = (ΔW_l, Δb_l). The head, log-std and critic are not projected.
(6) First-order change of every old head's σ-scaled mean on every anchor: c = Σ_l [rowsum((G_l ΔW_l) ⊙ Z_l) + G_l Δb_l] ∈ R^M.
(7) α = K^{-1} c. Then ΔW_l ← ΔW_l − G_l^T diag(α) Z_l, Δb_l ← Δb_l − G_l^T α, and θ = θ_prev + Δ. The projection is applied to Adam's output, not to the gradient: SGP found that projected gradients fed into Adam forget catastrophically in PPO. Adam's moments keep the raw gradients. Log ρ = ||Δ − Δ_proj||/||Δ||, the share of the step that conflicts.

After the update epochs:
(8) Restore. Recompute G, Z and K at the current θ on the same anchors. Let e = (μ_j*(x) − μ_j(x;θ))/σ_j and β = K^{-1} e. Update W_l += η_r G_l^T diag(β) Z_l and b_l += η_r G_l^T β, with η_r = 1. This is the minimum-norm Gauss-Newton step that cancels accumulated second-order drift.
(9) Logs:
- Old-function drift d = mean((μ_j − μ_j*)/σ_j)^2 on 2,048 held-out bank states, at every eval.
- Conflict map: w_n = Σ_a α_{n,a}^2 summed over steps, reported as the phase histogram of the top 5% of anchors.

Option --fn_warmup T: for the first T iterations only the new head, log-std and critic learn. The new head starts equal to the old head, so the earliest trunk steps lie mostly in the old head's row space and would be removed anyway. Default 0; ablation T = 5.

Chain: skill k protects every earlier head. M grows by 4,096 per old skill, and ρ per skill serves as the capacity meter.

Exploration, identical in every arm:
- A gripper std floor of 1.0 on the new skill's own log-std, applied only if the source's deterministic success on the new task is below 10% in a 256-episode probe before training. Exploration hurt where the source already succeeds.
- The floor is global, not local to the seam, because local and global tied in our data.
- The critic is separate and never constrained.

Cost and code:
- About 1.2 GMAC per Adam step, about 0.1 s per iteration, under 300 MB.
- About 150 lines in wrwl/ppo.py: projector, anchor sampler, restore and logs.
- About 70 more lines for the KL-replay and LoRA baselines.
methods.grounded_in:
(1) Full FT forgets 14-23 points of PickCube while its hidden weights move only 11-13%. Units picked by policy-gradient importance or by conflict do no better than random units. So parameter locality does not predict the damage; the change in the old outputs does, as RL's Razor also found. That is why this method protects outputs, not parameters.

(2) In function space the old skill is small: 8 action means on states that occupy 10/42 input directions and about 20/256 hidden directions. On 512 anchors its Jacobian has 4,096 rows, against 142,592 trunk parameters, so most of a PPO step should survive the projection. Under GPM projection, by contrast, 94-97% of the new skill's input energy is blocked.

(3) Gradient conflict is aligned on average but oscillates from step to step. The protection therefore has to be recomputed every step and every iteration, not fixed once as a unit mask.

(4) Conflict states (holding at the goal) sit on the old skill's densest region, so the multipliers α should concentrate there. This is a falsifiable by-product.

(5) An unverified clue from the BC probe: only 26% of the readout change fell inside the old subspace, against 54% for the control. New behaviour can be read from directions the old skill hardly uses.

(6) Exploration: the floor is the main lever, local tied global, and exploration hurt when the source already succeeds. Hence a global floor gated on source success.
methods.first_experiment:
Step 0. Post-hoc check of how much room the projection leaves (about 0.3 GPU-h; go/no-go).
(a) On today's 4 full-FT Stack checkpoints: the share of the actual update θ_FT − θ_Pick that lies in the row space of the Pick head's Jacobian at θ_Pick, on 4,096 Pick-bank anchors.
(b) On one rollout batch of the Pick expert in StackCubeNarrow: the share of the PPO trunk gradient that survives the function-null projection, against a GPM projection with Pick's 99% input subspaces. The survey predicts about 17-25% survives GPM.

Step 1. Pair Pick→StackCubeNarrow, today's protocol:
- stack_to_pick adapter, sparse reward, 1,024 envs × 50 steps, γ 0.95, floor 1.0;
- eval every 2 iterations with 256 episodes;
- '90%' = start of 3 consecutive evals ≥ 0.9; halt at 8M;
- seeds 1-4.

New arms (28 runs):
- M1-bank, M1-self, M1-bank + warmup 5;
- KL-replay on Pick-bank states at λ ∈ {0.3, 3}: loss += λ·mean Σ_a (μ_old − μ*)^2/2σ^2 on 2,048 bank states per minibatch;
- KL-LwF on Stack's own minibatch states, λ = 1;
- head-only at LR 1e-3, a control for effective step size. If it reaches 90% in ≤ 1.8M, this pair cannot separate any method from head-only, and screening moves to PlaceCube or PushRetreat-10.

Reused arms, after a bit-check of FT seed 1 under the new code with every flag off:
- FT + floor: 1.5M, retention 0.82-0.86;
- head-only: 3.1M, retention 0.992;
- 5% and 20% units.

Step 2. Chains Pick→Stack→PlaceCube and Pick→PlaceCube→Stack, seeds 1-3.
- Arms: FT, best KL arm, M1-bank. Skill 3 continues from that arm's own skill-2 checkpoint; the floor applies only if the source's success on the new task is below 10%.
- Runs: 9 PlaceCube skill-2 runs and 18 skill-3 runs.

Metrics:
- New-skill steps to 90%.
- Retention: deterministic success of every earlier skill through the current trunk with its own head, 1,024 episodes. retention_eval.py needs extending to Stack and PlaceCube views.
- Actor parameters added per skill.
- ρ, drift d, and the conflict map's phase histogram.

Decision:
- GO (FN-PPO becomes the headline) if all of these hold: median steps ≤ 1.8M (≤ 1.2× FT); retention ≥ 0.98 in every seed; faster than every KL arm that keeps ≥ 0.98; and in the chain, both earlier skills ≥ 0.97 after skill 3.
- Zero-growth Pareto point only, if retention is ≥ 0.98 but steps fall in 1.8-2.2M.
- KILL if retention < 0.97 (the projection leaks) or steps > 2.2M. At that speed it is no better than 5% units, which also keep 0.97-0.99.

Screening uses 4 seeds; headline cells later get 10 seeds with rliable IQM and 95% bootstrap CIs.

Compute: about 2 GPU-h for the pair, 2.5 GPU-h for the chains and 1 GPU-h for evals, so about 6 GPU-h, or 3-4 h wall time.
- haha-a (free, as the user said): 4 concurrent Stack jobs.
- haha-d (31 GB RAM): 4 Stack jobs or 3 PlaceCube jobs at a time.
- haha-c stays clear for the lab's EVO job and the a2r port.
- Runs shared with OccSplit and ConflictSplit (KL arms, FT bit-check, chain FT) are counted once.
methods.a2r_path:
Everything goes in our private copy (~/zhr_pve). The lab's repo, envs and caches are never touched.

What is shared and what is private:
- Shared: the five Linear layers of actor.trunk (a 323→512 projection and four 512×512 ResBlock Linears; about 1.22M parameters).
- Frozen: PointNet, task encoder, proprio norm and the LayerNorm affines, as in the planned F0 arm.
- Private: a new actor.head (512→7) initialised from S1's, log_std and the critic.
- Old skill = S1, i.e. insert_key with require_turn=False. S1 and T share the interaction id, so separate heads are required.

Projection:
- Anchors: 20k S1 rollout states on the training reset distribution, stored as obs dicts (about 75 MB).
- G_l and Z_l come from forward and backward hooks with 7 one-hot cotangents; N = 256 gives M = 1,792. The Hadamard Gram applies because each Linear is applied once per sample; the per-point PointNet Linears are not, so they stay frozen.
- Projection runs after each of the 20 Adam steps per iteration (5 epochs × 4 minibatches), about 9 GFLOP each.
- LR is fixed. a2r's adaptive rate would rise as the projection shrinks the realised KL.

Gate R0, before any method run: the stock F-plain warm start on insert+turn must drop S1's insertion success through S1's head by at least 5 pp (512 near starts plus 1,024 training starts). Otherwise the 512-wide trunk already forgets too little (the Simple-Recipe regime) and the pair becomes a negative control.

Arms: F-plain, F-plain + KL-replay, FN-PPO, each with the dim-5 (turn) std floor only if V1 (S1's success on T) is below 10%. 3 seeds, judged by the E-13 paired-CI rule.

Compute: one Isaac job per GPU at about 2-3k steps/s, so about 1.5-3 h per run on haha-c or haha-d.

methods.name: OccSplit: train as plain full fine-tuning, keep the part of the update that lands on the old skills' occupied subspace private
methods.idea:
The new skill trains exactly like full fine-tuning with the floor, the fastest trainer we have. Its update is then stored so that the old skills cannot see it. An old skill feels a change to a layer's weights only through the directions its own inputs to that layer occupy (Pick: 10/42 input, about 20/256 hidden at 99% energy). Each layer's update ΔW is therefore split in two:
- ΔW·P_U lies inside the old skills' occupied subspace. It is kept private to the new skill as an out×k map.
- ΔW·(I − P_U) is free capacity. It is merged into the shared weights, where by construction no old skill can see it.

The new skill's network equals the fine-tuned network exactly. Old skills keep their function up to the occupancy residual. Training needs no old data and no Jacobians; the old skill's state set is used once, to compute its occupied subspace. Because the split is linear in a fixed basis, it can be applied after training to any trained network, including a scratch-trained one for a reversed skill.

This is the 'unshare the occupied space, share the free capacity' reading of the user's idea.
methods.algorithm:
Occupancy memory, computed once per skill when its training ends:
- Run the skill's own deterministic policy through its own view (shared weights plus its private parts) and collect 4,096 states, stratified by phase. Record the input z_{l-1} of each trunk Linear.
- Layer 1 is standardised per dimension: z̃ = z/r, where r is the RMS over all stored skills' states. Raw energy would drop small but crucial inputs such as tcp_to_obj near the cube. Hidden layers (tanh outputs) are used as they are.
- Union second moment, each skill weighted equally: C_l = Σ_j (1/|S_j|) Σ_{x∈S_j} z̃ z̃^T.
- Take eigenvectors U_l (in × k_l). k_l is the smallest k for which the WORST state's residual ||(I − U U^T) z̃||^2/||z̃||^2 is ≤ ε over all stored states. ε ∈ {1e-2, 1e-3, 1e-4}, default 1e-3. Worst-state rather than average energy keeps rare at-goal states covered.
- U_l grows by appending orthonormalised new directions. Earlier columns stay fixed, so stored private maps stay valid. No raw states are kept.

Adding skill k:
(a) Reuse race. Run 0.3M-step branches from the view of each candidate source skill and from scratch, using a fresh init as in today's PullCube scratch arm. Keep the branch with the highest training success at 0.3M; on a tie, reuse.
(b) Train that branch with unchanged wrwl/ppo.py: all trunk parameters, a private head, a private log-std and a private critic, under the exploration rule below. This is literally today's full-FT arm. Stop at the 90% rule.
(c) Split each trunk Linear l, with Δ_l = W_l^{(k)} − W_l^{sh}:
- private map A_l^{(k)} = Δ_l R U_l (out × k_l), where R = diag(r) for layer 1 and the identity otherwise;
- shared update W_l^{sh} ← W_l^{sh} + Δ_l R (I − U_l U_l^T) R^{-1};
- biases are entirely private, because the constant input is occupied by every skill.
(d) Skill k runs on W_l^{sh} + A_l^{(k)} U_l^T R^{-1}, b_l^{sh} + Δb_l^{(k)}, and head k. This equals the trained network exactly.
- Old skill j runs on W_l^{sh} + A_l^{(j)} U_l^T R^{-1}. Its layer inputs lie in span(U_l) up to ε.
- So the merged free part changes its pre-activations by at most ||Δ_l||·√ε·||z̃||. At ε = 1e-3 and the measured 11-13% weight change, that is about 0.4% of the pre-activation scale.
(e) Add skill k's states, seen through skill k's view, to the occupancy memory.

The split is linear with a fixed U, so the online version (a shadow θ^{sh} += s·R(I − U U^T)R^{-1} after every Adam step) and the post-hoc version give the same result. The post-hoc version needs no change to training at all.

Exploration: the same rule as every arm. A gripper (or new-action-dim) std floor of 1.0 applies only if the chosen branch's initial deterministic success on the new task is below 10%. In the chains this switches the floor off for PlaceCube from Stack, since the Stack policy already releases. There is no seam-local placement. The critic is per skill and unconstrained.

Parameters added per skill: Σ_l 256·k_l, plus 768 for biases, plus 2,064 for head and std. At today's 99%-energy occupancy (k = 10, 21, 18) that is 15.4k, or 10.6% of the actor. For comparison, LoRA r=16 adds 23.2k and a full copy (FT-N) 144.7k.

Code: about 120 lines.
- Occupancy memory.
- Split and library save/load: shared trunk, per-skill heads, private maps and the basis.
- retention_eval over library views.
- A --gpm flag that applies the same projector to the training step, as a baseline.
methods.grounded_in:
(1) The old skill occupies few directions per layer (99% energy: 10/42 input, about 20/256 hidden, 58/256 at the last hidden layer). Its function therefore depends on the shared weights only through W·U.
(2) 94-97% of the new skill's activation energy lies inside U. That is why input-subspace protection (GPM) should starve learning, and why the occupied part has to stay trainable, privately.
(3) Full FT with the floor is the fastest trainer we have: 1.5M steps, against 1.75M for 20% units and 3.1M for head-only. So the method must not touch its dynamics.
(4) In the BC probe, the FT update is spread over about 190/256 units and is no more concentrated than a random-target control. Unit masks cannot isolate it; a split along directions of the old skill's own input subspace can.
(5) Reversed skills: on PullCube, scratch reaches 90% in 1.2M while every reuse arm needs more than 7M or never gets there. The split must therefore accept a scratch-trained network, and a linear split by occupancy does that exactly.
(6) Exploration follows the data: a global floor, gated on source success.
methods.differs_from:
- GPM, Adam-NSCL and InfLoRA restrict the TRAINING update to the complement of the old subspace (InfLoRA via a fixed down-projection onto new directions there) and discard the occupied part. With our overlap that means head-only speed. OccSplit never constrains training and keeps the occupied part privately.
- TRGP gives the new task a private k×k scaling inside the old subspace, so its outputs are limited to span(W·B). OccSplit's private map is out×k, fully expressive on those inputs.
- TAIL and per-skill LoRA learn a delta on a frozen trunk under a training-time rank constraint with a learned down-projection. OccSplit trains unconstrained, fixes the down-projection to the measured old occupancy, and keeps growing the shared weights with the free part.
- Model merging with per-task masks (TALL-masks, EMR-Merging) and AlphaEdit-style null-space edits protect a base model by projecting task vectors and dropping or rescaling the rest. OccSplit keeps the projected-out part as the new skill's private map, so neither side loses function.
- Reset & Distill needs a distillation phase for scratch skills. OccSplit grafts the scratch network exactly.
- CLARE adds capacity by feature novelty, which would mark Pick→Stack as 'share all'. The OccSplit criterion is the old skill's own occupancy.
methods.first_experiment:
Step 0: post-hoc, no training, about 1.5 GPU-h. This step alone can decide.
- Inputs: today's 4 full-FT Stack checkpoints (early-stopped at 90%; retention 0.82-0.86).
- Compute U from 4,096 Pick-bank states for ε ∈ {1e-2, 1e-3, 1e-4} × {raw, standardised layer 1}, plus the plain 99%-average-energy U as a check on the worst-state criterion.
- Measure:
  - Pick retention through the shared view: old head, 1,024 deterministic episodes.
  - Stack success of the private view. It must equal FT up to float rounding; this is a sanity check.
  - Private parameter count.
  - Maximum pre-activation leak on held-out Pick states.
- Post-hoc baselines on the same checkpoints:
  - RETAIN interpolation, α ∈ {0.25, 0.5, 0.75}: Stack via the new head, Pick via the old head.
  - SVD-truncated FT delta at matched private size, r ∈ {8, 16, 32}: Pick exact, Stack measured.

Step 1: training, 4 seeds, about 1.5 GPU-h.
- GPM with the same U applied as a training constraint. Prediction: about 3M steps.
- Per-skill LoRA r=16 on the frozen trunk, at LR 3e-4 and 1e-3.
- These give the speed of the zero-forgetting alternatives.

Step 2: reversed pair, post-hoc plus logs, about 0.5 GPU-h.
- Graft today's scratch PullCube checkpoints (seed 1; rerun seeds 2-3 at about 10 min each if missing) into the Push expert.
- Measure Push retention through the shared view (1,024 episodes), Pull success (equals scratch) and private size.
- From existing train.csv files, check that a 0.3M-step race would have picked scratch for Pull and reuse for Stack.

Step 3: chains, about 2 GPU-h.
- Pick→Stack→PlaceCube and Pick→PlaceCube→Stack, seeds 1-3.
- Skill 3 is trained as FT from skill 2's view (floor gated by source success) and split with the union occupancy.
- Measure retention of skills 1 and 2 after skill 3, and private size per skill.
- These FT runs also carry ConflictSplit's shadows.

Metrics:
- Steps to 90%: equal to FT by construction; verify.
- Retention of each earlier skill.
- Parameters added per skill.
- Leak.

Decision:
- GO if some ε gives retention ≥ 0.98 in all 4 seeds with a private part ≤ 15% of the actor (Σk ≤ 73 across layers), and the chains keep both earlier skills ≥ 0.97.
- It must also beat LoRA r=16 on steps at equal retention, and beat RETAIN and SVD-FT on the speed-retention-parameters Pareto.
- KILL, falling back to ConflictSplit, if retention is < 0.97 even at ε = 1e-4 or the private part exceeds 30%.

Full paper: 5 skills, adding StackRetreat (about 20 lines, like PushRetreat) and PushCube through a 10-line push_to_pick adapter. The latter is the different-family skill that exercises the race.

Total: about 5.5 GPU-h. Step 0 goes on haha-a first, after copying runs/units/*/final_ckpt.pt from c and d and data/bc_pick_c1.pt. Training steps go on haha-a and haha-d.
methods.a2r_path:
Everything runs in our private copy only.

Occupancy:
- Computed from 4,096 S1 (insert-only) states on the training starts, with worst-state ε = 1e-3.
- It covers the inputs of the five trunk Linears: the 323-d concat (PointNet feature, normalised proprio, task embedding) and four 512-d post-LN-SiLU inputs.

Training:
- Train insert+turn with the lab's stock F-plain warm start and the dim-5 floor gated by V1.
- This changes no training dynamics at all, so it is the safest port.
- PointNet stays frozen if F-plain still learns the turn. Otherwise its per-point Linears are split the same way and will most likely end up private (about 42k parameters).

Split after training:
- Private: Δ·U U^T per Linear (512 × k_l), plus biases, LayerNorm affines and the new head.
- Shared: the free part is added to the shared weights.
- The residual stream stays safe. For S1's inputs the free part of each ResBlock's output Linear contributes zero, so S1's stream is unchanged.

Evaluation:
- Retention: S1 insert success (require_turn=False) through S1's head on the shared view, on 512 near starts plus 1,024 training starts.
- T success equals F-plain's by construction.
- Same R0 gate (F-plain must forget at least 5 pp) and E-13 3-seed rule.

Cost: only the F-plain runs (about 1.5-3 h each, one per GPU) plus minutes of eval.

methods.name: ConflictSplit: full fine-tuning whose function-space conflict is routed to a private delta; everything else, even inside the old skills' space, stays shared
methods.idea:
This is the literal form of 'find which parts of the old skill's space the new skill can share, and unshare only where they conflict'.
- The new skill trains as plain full fine-tuning.
- A shadow copy of the shared weights (what the old skills see) receives each Adam step after FN-PPO's function-null projection, computed at the shadow.
- The function-safe part of every step therefore stays shared. That includes changes on the old skills' occupied inputs that write into directions their heads ignore, or into units that are off on their states.
- Only the conflicting component accumulates in the new skill's private delta.

That private delta is a direct measurement of the conflict: its norm, its rank, and which old states it protects. Stored as a rank-r factor, it is the smallest private part that keeps old skills exact while the new skill keeps full-FT speed.

It tests the user's 'few conflicting directions' hypothesis at the direction level, after the unit-level version failed (importance = random).
methods.algorithm:
Modules:
- The actor's weights are the new skill's effective weights θ^eff. They are trained by unchanged PPO with the floor, exactly as in the full-FT arm.
- A shadow θ^sh (trunk only) is what every old skill sees, through its own frozen head (and its own private delta in a chain).
- Private delta δ = θ^eff − θ^sh.
- At the start, θ^sh = θ^eff = θ_0 (the source view) and δ = 0.

Per iteration: anchors, G_l, Z_l and K exactly as in FN-PPO steps (1)-(4), but evaluated at θ^sh with every old head (bank or self anchors). Anchor sampling uses its own generator, so action noise and minibatch order are untouched and the new skill's run stays bit-identical to FT.

Per Adam step:
- s = θ^eff_after − θ^eff_before (trunk weights and biases).
- c = Σ_l [rowsum((G_l s_{W,l}) ⊙ Z_l) + G_l s_{b,l}].
- α = K^{-1} c.
- s^sh_l = s_l − [G_l^T diag(α) Z_l, G_l^T α].
- θ^sh += s^sh. In effect δ += s − s^sh, the conflict component.
- Log the conflict share ||s − s^sh||/||s||.

After the epochs: θ^sh += J^+ e, with e = (μ_j* − μ_j(θ^sh))/σ_j (the Gauss-Newton restore). This moves only the split; θ^eff is unchanged.

End of skill:
- Per layer, take the SVD of δ_l.
- Conflict rank r_l = the smallest rank whose truncation costs ≤ 1 point of the new skill's deterministic success when its view is θ^sh + rank-r(δ). Search r ∈ {2, 4, 8, 16, 32}.
- Store δ_l ≈ B_l C_l^T, i.e. r_l(out + in) parameters, plus the bias residual, head and std.
- Optional 'heal' if truncation costs more than 1 point: 3 PPO iterations on B, C and the head only, with θ^sh frozen.

Post-hoc version for existing checkpoints (no training):
- Set θ^sh ← θ^FT.
- Run 30 Gauss-Newton restores, each on a fresh batch of 512 anchor states: θ^sh ← θ^sh + J^+(μ* − μ(θ^sh)).
- δ = θ^FT − θ^sh is the minimum-norm change that must stay private for the old skill to be exact.

Diagnostics:
- Conflict share ||δ||/||θ^FT − θ_0||.
- Per-layer rank of δ at 90% and 99% energy, compared with the FT update's rank of 10-23.
- Share of δ's input side inside OccSplit's U (≤ 1 by construction), and of its output side inside the head-read directions.
- Conflict map from α: phase histogram of the anchors.

Chain: anchors for old skill j are evaluated through j's own view (θ^sh + compressed δ_j, kept fixed). The Jacobian is taken with respect to θ^sh only.

Reuse gate: the same 0.3M race as OccSplit. A scratch winner is grafted with OccSplit's split, because first-order routing does not apply to a scratch delta.

Exploration and critic: as in the other methods.

Code: about 60 lines on top of FN-PPO's projector (the shadow, compression and a post-hoc GN script).
methods.grounded_in:
(1) Occupancy is necessary but not sufficient. The old head reads only 8 of the 58 occupied last-hidden directions. Tanh units that are saturated or off on old states have D ≈ 0. So the subspace where the skills conflict in function should be much smaller than the occupied one; this is testable as rank(δ) much smaller than k. In the a2r trunk, LayerNorm + SiLU make this gap larger.
(2) Gradient conflict is aligned on average but oscillates step to step, so the split has to be computed at every step, not from a single mask.
(3) Picking units by conflict or by importance is no better than random, so conflict has to be defined in function space and per direction, not per unit.
(4) Conflict states sit on the old skill's densest region, so a few anchors there should carry most of α. This links our representation finding to a mechanism instead of an analysis section.
(5) Full FT is the fastest trainer, so the new skill's dynamics must stay untouched; the shadow guarantees that bit for bit.
(6) Full FT moves the hidden weights 11-13% and forgets 14-23 points. The post-hoc restore asks how small a part of that move has to stay private to undo the forgetting.
methods.differs_from:
- FN-PPO and OGD discard the conflicting component, so the new skill must find another route; they add no private parameters. ConflictSplit keeps that component privately, so the new skill trains at full-FT speed.
- OccSplit makes the whole occupied input subspace private. ConflictSplit makes private only the part that changes old outputs, so changes inside the occupied space that old heads cannot see stay shared and reusable by later skills.
- TRGP and CUBER pick a 'private scaling inside the old subspace' regime per old task and layer, once per task, using projection-norm and gradient-cosine thresholds. ConflictSplit decides per Adam step, in function space, with no thresholds.
- Memory Anchors (IL) finds conflict states in order to replay them. Here the conflict states fall out of the projection multipliers, and the conflict is stored as parameters, not replayed.
- PackNet and CoTASP allocate units; units are the wrong axis on our data.
- Reset & Distill always resets. Here reuse is the default, and the scratch route only enters through the race.
methods.first_experiment:
Step 0: post-hoc, about 1 GPU-h. This step decides the user's 'few conflicting directions' claim.
- Inputs: today's 4 full-FT Stack checkpoints.
- Run 30 Gauss-Newton restores against the Pick snapshot, each on 512 fresh Pick-bank anchors (M = 4,096).
- Measure:
  - Pick retention of θ^sh (1,024 episodes);
  - conflict share;
  - per-layer rank of δ at 90% and 99% energy;
  - Stack success of θ^sh + rank-r(δ) for r ∈ {2, 4, 8, 16};
  - anchor-phase histogram of |β|.

Step 1: online, seeds 1-4, about 1.2 GPU-h.
- 4 new FT runs, each carrying two shadows (bank anchors and self anchors).
- The Stack curve must reproduce the FT curve exactly: bit-check against a run without shadows, seed 1.
- Measure retention of each shadow at the 90% checkpoint and the conflict rank.
- OccSplit's post-hoc split is computed from the same runs.

Step 2: chains, hosted in OccSplit's chain FT runs; about 0.5 GPU-h of extra evals.
- Pick→Stack→PlaceCube and the reverse order, seeds 1-3.
- Measure retention of skills 1 and 2 through their shadows after skill 3, and private rank per skill.
- Shadow cost is under 5% per iteration.

Comparisons at matched private parameters: OccSplit, LoRA r=16, SVD-truncated FT delta, KL-replay (shared runs) and FN-PPO.

Metrics:
- Steps to 90%, equal to FT by construction.
- Retention of each earlier skill.
- Private parameters after compression.
- Conflict rank and conflict share.

Decision:
- GO, with the headline 'the conflict is a few directions, stored privately; everything else shared', if retention ≥ 0.98 in all seeds and the compressed private part costs ≤ 1 point of Stack success while being at most half of OccSplit's private size at equal retention. For reference, rank 8 per layer comes to 13.4k actor parameters including the head (9.3%).
- If rank(δ) is about the FT update's rank (10-23), the concentration hypothesis also fails at the direction level. Report that as a finding, and let OccSplit, which is simpler and needs no replay, carry the method.
- KILL if θ^sh retention is < 0.97, meaning first-order routing leaks.

Compute: about 3 GPU-h beyond the shared runs. Post-hoc work goes on haha-a, online runs on haha-a and haha-d.
methods.a2r_path:
This uses the same anchor bank, hooks and Gram machinery as FN-PPO's port, in our private copy only.
- The shadow is updated after each of a2r's 20 Adam steps per iteration while F-plain trains unchanged. This carries no risk to the lab's recipe, and the adaptive LR is untouched because the trained weights are F-plain's.
- LayerNorm affines and biases are kept private. PointNet is frozen or made private.

The a2r trunk is where ConflictSplit should beat OccSplit on parameters. Pre-norm LayerNorm + SiLU blocks keep many directions active on S1's inputs that S1's 7 action means do not depend on. So δ should be far smaller than OccSplit's 512 × k_l maps; the measurement checks this.

Evaluation:
- Retention: S1 insertion success through S1's head on θ^sh.
- T: θ^sh + δ, equal to F-plain.
- R0 gate and E-13 rule as above.

Cost: under 5% extra per iteration on top of the F-plain runs.

verdicts.method: FN-PPO: project every Adam step onto the null space of the old skills' outputs (zero growth)
verdicts.verdict: Already done? As an algorithm, yes; as an RL recipe, no prior found. A reviewer will read it as OGD-ALL's output-gradient null space, recomputed GEM-style at the current weights from a memory, with SGP's projection of Adam's output and a Gauss-Newton correction. The Hadamard Gram (G G^T) ⊙ (Z Z^T + 1) is the known ghost-norm / NTK identity. None of the parts is new. What we did not find is a paper that applies a function-space (output-Jacobian) hard projection to continual or stage-extension RL. The two RL null-space precedents both protect input-activation subspaces: SGP (PPO on Atari) and NSPO (GRPO on LLMs, Dec 2025, subspace computed once before training). Real novelty margin: (a) the measured claim that in stage extension, input-space protection leaves only the 3-6% residual of the step (head-only speed) while function-space protection leaves most of it, so a zero-growth shared trunk can reach near-FT speed at >=0.98 retention; (b) an old-data-free 'self-anchor' variant, which works because the new task's on-policy states contain the old skill's prefix. The margin is moderate if Step 0 shows a large gap in surviving step share and Step 1 beats KL-replay at equal retention. Otherwise it is thin: 'OGD works in PPO'.
verdicts.closest_prior: All links checked 2026-11-01. (1) OGD, Farajtabar et al., AISTATS 2020, https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.07104: the same null space of output gradients. It is supervised, stores gradients once per task and uses SGD. NTK analysis / OGD+: https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.11942. (2) GEM, Lopez-Paz & Ranzato, NIPS 2017, https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.08840: re-evaluates memory gradients at the current weights every step and projects through a dual QP. Its dual variables play the role of your alpha, but there is one constraint per task loss rather than per output. (3) SGP, Saha & Roy, AAAI 2023, https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.01386: PPO on 6 Atari games, projection applied to Adam's output, GPM input bases with importance scaling. (4) NSPO, arXiv Dec 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.11391: GRPO policy gradient projected onto the null space of the input covariance on general data (AlphaEdit-style), computed once. This is the nearest 'RL + null space to keep old abilities', and its name is close to yours. (5) Soft function-space neighbours: FROMP, NeurIPS 2020, https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.14070. C-CHAIN, ICML 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.00592: a continual-RL penalty on output churn over reference batches. CPO 'RL Forgets!', arXiv Jul 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.04364: a replay-free Fisher surrogate of behavioural KL for LLM/VLM RL. Hidekel & Raviv, arXiv Jun 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18024: a penalty on the top NTK eigenmodes of old outputs, supervised. GPM, ICLR 2021, https://openreview.net/forum?id=3AOj0RCNC2. (6) Machinery: the ghost-norm Gram identity, Li et al., ICLR 2022, https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.05679. Gauss-Newton steps under retain-set output constraints: K-FADE, arXiv Feb 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.10568. (7) Soft-replay baselines reviewers will demand: Wolczyk et al., ICML 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.02868. ACCRUE, arXiv Oct 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18596: Isaac Lab FORGE/AutoMate insertion, the direct competitor on a2r. Memory Anchors, CoRL 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26545. Progress & Compress, https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.06370.
verdicts.risks:
- The differs_from text overclaims and reads as unaware of the field. It says CHAIN is single-task, but C-CHAIN (ICML 2025) is continual RL. It omits NSPO, GEM and FROMP. 'Refresh at the current weights' is GEM's, and the Gram trick is ghost clipping's.
- If the ablation ladder (fixed end-of-skill gradients -> refresh every iteration -> projection of Adam's output -> restore) shows that no rung matters, the paper reduces to 'OGD in PPO', a weak method claim for RSS.
- A speed problem is built into the design. The new head starts as a copy of the old head, so on states shared with the anchors the new skill's trunk gradient lies inside the protected row space and is projected away. Early training then behaves like head-only (3.1M) until the two heads diverge. The likely result falls in the 1.8-2.2M band, where 5% units already sit (2.2M, 0.97-0.99) with no Jacobians.
- Bank anchors are stored old-skill states, the same data assumption as ClonEx, ACCRUE and Memory Anchors. If KL-replay at lambda=3 on the same bank matches FN-PPO, the hard constraint buys nothing, and 'lambda -> infinity without stiffness' is unsupported.
- 'Zero growth' only matters under task ID with one head per skill. FT-N, a separate 145k-parameter copy, gets 1.5M steps and 0.992 retention trivially, so reviewers will ask why sharing matters at this scale. On a2r they will compare against ACCRUE directly.
- First-order equality on 512 anchors per iteration does not bound closed-loop drift on states outside the anchors. The restore reuses the same anchors, so it can overfit the constraint set.
verdicts.fixes:
1) Make Step 0(b) the paper's mechanism claim (about 0.3 GPU-h on haha-a). Measure the share of the PPO trunk step that survives function-null projection vs input-null projection (GPM bases, and an NSPO-style null space computed once) on Stack, PlaceCube and PushRetreat-10. Pre-register the ordering head-only ≈ GPM/NSPO-style < FN-PPO <= FT. This turns the occupancy analysis into a falsifiable mechanism and separates the method from SGP and NSPO.
2) Run OGD as published (output gradients stored at the end of Pick, projected gradient fed to Adam, no restore). Then add per-iteration refresh, projection of Adam's output and the restore one at a time. Claim only the rungs that measurably matter.
3) Lead with the self-anchor variant: in stage extension the new task's own on-policy states contain the old prefix. Compare it with KL-LwF, P&C-style distillation and C-CHAIN on the same states; 'old-data-free retention for stage-extension RL' is the slot nobody has claimed. If bank anchors beat self anchors by a wide margin, say plainly that the method is replay-class and beat KL-replay / ACCRUE-style distillation on the speed-retention frontier.
4) Turn alpha from a diagnostic into part of the method. Carry the top-|alpha| anchors across iterations, which gives a free detector of conflict states. Show it lowers the number of anchors M needed for 0.98 retention, and that those states coincide with Memory Anchors' latent-collapse states.
5) Deal with the head-copy symmetry. Log rho over time, and ablate --fn_warmup and a head initialisation that breaks the symmetry. If the gap to FT is not closed by about 0.3M steps, stop early.
6) Run the restore on fresh anchors, and measure drift on closed-loop rollouts, not only on anchor states.
7) Rewrite differs_from to cite NSPO, C-CHAIN, GEM, FROMP and K-FADE, and avoid a name close to NSPO. State the task-incremental scenario and put FT-N on the Pareto plot. On a2r, add an ACCRUE-style baseline that distils from retained episodes.

verdicts.method: OccSplit: train as plain full fine-tuning, keep the part of the update that lands on the old skills' occupied subspace private
verdicts.verdict: Already done? Not exactly, but a reviewer will likely call it an incremental recombination. The method splits an unconstrained FT update after training into two parts. The shared part, dW(I-P_U), is the GPM/AlphaEdit null-space projection; NUFILT (2025) already applies a post-hoc null-space filter of this kind to a fully fine-tuned task vector, though it discards the overlapping part. The private part, dW P_U, is TRGP's 'private map inside the old subspace' with the k x k scaling widened to an out x k block. Keeping the non-shareable part as a per-task routed expert is what Twin-Merging and ESM++ do in model merging. What no prior claims is the package: training dynamics untouched (the new skill is exactly FT), old skills certified to epsilon by worst-state occupancy, applied after training, and able to graft any network, including one trained from scratch. The margin is real but narrow. All of its value is parameter efficiency under task ID, so it will be judged against private SVD-compressed FT deltas, per-skill LoRA and FT-N rather than against GPM, and on Pick->Stack it may lose to SVD-FT. It is the least novel of the three, and the safest engineering baseline.
verdicts.closest_prior: All links checked 2026-11-01. (1) TRGP, Lin et al., ICLR 2022, https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.02931: shared weights updated orthogonally to the old input subspaces, plus a learned per-task scaling Q (k x k) on the old subspace. This is the same split, shared in the complement and private in the occupied part. CUBER, NeurIPS 2022, https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.00789. (2) NUFILT, arXiv Sep 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.21413: a post-hoc null-space filter of a fully fine-tuned task vector. The overlapping part is discarded and partly compensated by a data-free LoRA; there are no private parameters. (3) Restricting training to the free complement: GPM, https://openreview.net/forum?id=3AOj0RCNC2; Adam-NSCL, https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.07113; InfLoRA, CVPR 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.00228; NESS, CPAL 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21919; KeepLoRA, ICLR 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.19659; OrthoSkillVLA, PRCV 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19589 (robot imitation learning, with private decoder experts per skill); AlphaEdit, ICLR 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.02355; NSPO, https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.11391. (4) Shared + private decompositions: APD, ICLR 2020, https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.09432; DEN, ICLR 2018, https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.01547; LoDA, ICML 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00191 (task-shared vs isolated LoRA subspaces). (5) Merging that uses input statistics or keeps per-task experts: RegMean, ICLR 2023, https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.09849; CAT Merging, ICML 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06977; Twin-Merging, NeurIPS 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.15479; ESM/ESM++, arXiv 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19164. (6) Robot baselines: RETAIN, ICLR 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.08333; Reset & Distill, https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.05066.
verdicts.risks:
- SVD-FT will likely dominate on the abstract's pair. The FT update is low rank (10-23 directions per layer), and Pick's occupancy at the trunk-layer inputs is similar (k = 10/21/18 at 99% energy). Storing a private rank-16 to rank-23 SVD of the FT delta keeps old skills exact, not just within epsilon, at about the same storage, and may keep Stack within 1 pt. If so, OccSplit is Pareto-dominated exactly where it is supposed to shine.
- The worst-state epsilon = 1e-3 criterion can inflate k_l at the tanh layers, driven by rare at-goal states, and push the private part past the 30% KILL line. Meanwhile the U from 99% average energy may leak on exactly those states.
- The 'one network' claim does not survive review. This is parameter isolation with task ID. Union occupancy also grows along the chain, so each new skill's private cost rises until it is a full copy (progressive-network-like), which contradicts the RSI story of adding skills cheaply.
- Without a trained TRGP arm that shows out x k is needed, reviewers will call it 'TRGP with a full private block'.
- The leak bound is first-order and per layer, and it is measured on bank states. Compounding over a 50-step closed loop can still cost retention on states the 4,096-state bank does not cover.
- Naming: in RL, 'occupancy' means the state-action visitation measure, which will confuse reviewers.
verdicts.fixes:
1) Re-scope the headline to the case where only OccSplit is cheap: grafting high-rank deltas. The scratch-trained reversed skill (PullCube into the Push network) has a full-rank delta, so SVD-FT needs nearly a full copy, while OccSplit costs only out x k_Push. Claim: 'graft any policy, including one trained from scratch, at the cost of the old skills' occupancy; the new skill is exact and old skills are epsilon-certified'. Report Stack and PushRetreat as the regime where it ties SVD-FT.
2) Always store the private map factored, at rank min(k_l, rank(dW R U)). Then it can never be larger than SVD-FT on the same delta. Plot private size against both quantities: the epsilon leak on old skills and the truncation loss on the new skill.
3) Add two arms that bracket OccSplit. A trained TRGP arm (k x k Q plus a GPM-shared update) tests whether out x k is needed. A NUFILT/GPM post-hoc filter arm (shared part only, overlapping part discarded) tests whether the private part is needed at all.
4) Report a capacity law: how many new union directions each skill adds per layer, and the private size per skill along a 4-5-skill chain. Frame it honestly as 'copy-on-write in activation coordinates', an engineering contribution, not RSI-style sharing.
5) Pick epsilon from the retention-versus-size curve, and validate the leak on closed-loop rollouts. Rename the method (e.g., SubspaceSplit or CoW-Skills) to avoid the clash with RL's occupancy measure.

verdicts.method: ConflictSplit: full fine-tuning whose function-space conflict is routed to a private delta; everything else, even inside the old skills' space, stays shared
verdicts.verdict: Already done? No direct prior found; this is the most novel of the three. No paper routes the function-space-conflicting component of each optimizer step into a private per-skill delta while the new skill's training stays bit-identical to FT. Each neighbour has one ingredient: OGD/FN-PPO discard the conflict; DEN duplicates units whose drift crosses a threshold; Recon unshares whole layers with high gradient conflict; IGFA (Jul 2026, supervised) protects conflicting directions and shares aligned ones but has no private parameters; TRGP, CUBER and LoDA pick shared vs isolated subspaces per task or layer by thresholds. The post-hoc variant (Gauss-Newton restore toward the old function, keep the residual) uses known machinery: K-FADE-style retain-set GN steps and NUFILT-style post-hoc filtering. The margin is moderate as a mechanism and potentially strong as a finding, but only if the measured conflict really is small. If it is spread out, the method collapses into OccSplit/SVD-FT. And the general claim that interference is low-rank in function space is already argued in supervised 2026 work (Hidekel & Raviv; E2-LoRA).
verdicts.closest_prior: All links checked 2026-11-01. (1) IGFA, Störk, arXiv Jul 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09202: 'share when aligned, protect when conflicting' at the direction level. It is supervised, uses a single shared head and a threshold gate, and has no private parameters. (2) DEN, ICLR 2018, https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.01547: duplicates units whose drift crosses a threshold so that old tasks keep the old copy, i.e. unit-level copy-on-conflict. (3) Recon, ICLR 2023, https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.11289: turns the layers with the highest gradient-conflict scores into task-specific layers (multi-task learning, layer level, network retrained). (4) OGD, https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.07104, and your FN-PPO: the same projector, with the conflict discarded. (5) Shared vs isolated subspaces: TRGP, https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.02931; CUBER, https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.00789; LoDA, ICML 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00191. (6) Restore and filter machinery: K-FADE, arXiv Feb 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.10568; NUFILT, https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.21413. (7) Gradient routing: CIDER, arXiv Aug 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.21899 (stop-gradient routing on a shared adapter; SAC/RLPD; distillation on stored archives; real robot). Gradient Routing, Cloud et al. 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.04332 (data-dependent gradient masks that localise capabilities, including in an RL policy). (8) Low-rank-interference claims and conflict states: Hidekel & Raviv, https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18024; E2-LoRA, ICML 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27482; Memory Anchors, CoRL 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26545.
verdicts.risks:
- The headline result can come out negative. You already found the FT update is no more concentrated than a random-target control. Also, with the head-copy init, much of the early trunk motion changes what the shared head reads, which is conflict by definition. So the conflict share rho may be large and delta spread out. If rank_99(delta) comes out near the FT update's 10-23, the 'few conflicting directions' hypothesis also fails at the direction level.
- The delta that the GN restore and projection produce has minimum Frobenius norm, not minimum rank. Its rank is bounded by the span of the anchors' layer inputs and by the backprop span, not by rank(dW_FT). It can therefore come out higher-rank than the FT update even when a low-rank solution exists.
- The GO bar 'at most half of OccSplit's private size' is weak. Delta's input side lies in the span of the anchors' layer inputs, which is roughly the old occupancy, so delta is already about as small as OccSplit's private part by construction. The meaningful competitor is the SVD-truncated FT delta at equal new-skill success.
- The online shadow depends on the training path, and first-order routing at each step can leak. If the post-hoc delta is as good, reviewers will ask why the shadow exists. Any 'heal' iterations void the claim of FT speed by construction.
- The same task-ID / FT-N objection applies. A shared trunk only beats per-skill deltas if later skills learn faster from it, and that has not yet been shown.
- The name sits close to CAT (Conflict-Aware Task) Merging and Recon. Define 'conflict' explicitly as a function-space change on the old heads.
verdicts.fixes:
1) Make Step 0 the go/no-go gate (post-hoc GN on the 4 FT checkpoints, haha-a) and pre-register the claim. Success means: rank_99(delta_l) <= 1/3 of the FT update's rank in every layer, AND Stack within 1 pt at rank <= 4, AND Pick retention >= 0.98. That gives a headline that DEN, Recon and IGFA never measured in RL: 'the conflict between a skill and its extension is a few function-space directions; the rest of the update is shareable'.
2) Search for a low-rank delta directly instead of the minimum-norm one. Either run rank-r-truncated GN iterations (truncate delta to rank r, re-restore theta_sh, repeat) or add a nuclear-norm penalty to the restore, and sweep r.
3) Make the post-hoc version the method (FT -> GN projection onto the old-function manifold -> rank-r residual), and keep the online shadow only if it beats post-hoc. If delta turns out low-rank, the natural trainable form is a rank-r private 'conflict absorber' trained jointly while the shared trunk receives function-null-projected steps. Present that version and compare it with TRGP and LoDA.
4) Show that sharing pays. In the 3-skill chains, skill 3 should learn faster from theta_sh than from a frozen trunk with LoRA or SVD-FT deltas. Without this forward transfer, per-skill deltas are simpler.
5) Connect to Memory Anchors. Show that the mass of |beta| / alpha, and delta's input side, concentrate on holding-at-goal states, i.e. 'parameter-space anchors stored as delta instead of replayed'.
6) Present the methods as one dial on a single Pareto plot of parameters, retention and steps: FN-PPO (delta = 0), ConflictSplit (delta = function-space conflict), OccSplit (delta = the whole occupied part) and FT-N (delta = the full update). Framed as a family, the work is more novel than any single arm and survives any one arm failing.

verdicts.method: FN-PPO: project every Adam step onto the null space of the old skills' outputs (zero growth)
verdicts.verdict: PLAUSIBLE. The best-supported of the three; run it first, with two changes (see fixes). Evidence from offline checks (Pick bank, all 39,647 kept states; held-out set = episodes with ep%5==0; 6 full-FT Stack checkpoints): (1) The old skill's function-space constraint is small. The Gram of 4,096 rows (512 phase-stratified anchors x 8 dims) holds 99% of its trace in 130 eigen-directions and 99.9% in 516. (2) Forgetting is visible to first order. The function-null part of the actual full-FT update (about 70% of its norm^2) barely moves Pick: held-out drift 0.10-0.62 sigma^2 and mean clipped arm-action change 0.008-0.023. The row-space part alone reproduces all of FT's damage: drift 9.6-17.5, arm change 0.084-0.128. (3) 512 anchors generalise: after projection, 0.3-0.5% of the first-order old-output change is left on 4,096 held-out states (0.1-0.2% with 1,024 anchors). (4) BC mini-replica of the conflict: teach the Stack gripper release on held-at-goal states; new head copied from Pick's; Adam 3e-4; 1,500 steps of 1,600 states. Final conflict loss / old drift: FN projecting gradient + step 1.60 / 0.21; FN step-only (as specified) 2.16 / 0.18; FT 1.82 / 3.36; head-only 4.53 / 0. In the same replica the Kronecker 'block' projector at 0.9 energy did not protect: drift 4.02 step-only, 3.16 with gradient projection. This matches the RL block arms: seed-1 retention 0.98 at 0.9 but 0.84 / 0.87 / 0.64 at 0.95 / 0.95r / 0.99, against FT 0.86. So the block results are not evidence against FN-PPO; an exact row space is what matters. Speed in RL is unproven: at init, 99.6% of the raw new-skill gradient lies in the old row space (copied head, and the conflict sits on Pick's densest states). The trunk can only progress through Adam-normalised leftover directions and through the private head moving away from the copy.
verdicts.closest_prior: OGD (Farajtabar et al., AISTATS 2020). Its OGD-ALL variant stores every output's Jacobian on memory samples and projects SGD steps onto their null space. Also GEM/A-GEM and OWM. The soft RL counterpart is KL/BC replay on old states: Wolczyk et al. ICML 2024 'Fine-tuning RL models is secretly a forgetting mitigation problem', ClonEx 2022, Progress & Compress 2018. The existing --protect_old block arm is the hard limit of Kronecker-factored Laplace (Ritter et al. 2018; NCL, Kao et al. 2021). Input-side relatives: GPM, Adam-NSCL, SGP, TRGP. Possibly new: per-iteration refresh from a simulation bank, the Hadamard Gram, projecting Adam's realised step, the Gauss-Newton restore, and RL stage-extension evidence. The linear algebra is not new.
verdicts.risks: (1) Adam moments. Step 7 of the spec keeps raw gradients in Adam's moments. Two results argue against that: the parent's smoke test (block, step-only drift 1.15 vs 0.26 with gradient projection) and my replica (FN step-only learns about 35% slower at equal protection). With the near-exact rows, step-only still protected, so the leak mechanism hurts approximate projectors most. (2) Speed under PPO noise. Because the raw gradient is 99.6% in the row space at init, advantage noise could push t90 toward block099's 2.25M or head-only's 3.1M; GO needs <= 1.8M. (3) The Gauss-Newton restore with eta_r = 1 is unstable from large drift. Starting from the FT checkpoints it diverged on 2 of 4 (drift rose to 55-299 mid-run); with step halving it converged on all 4. The restore is also an unclipped move of the shared trunk, which can shift the new skill outside PPO's trust region. (4) The ablation could collapse the paper claim: if FT plus a damped per-iteration restore, with no per-step projection, matches FN-PPO, the method is functional replay. (5) Retention is a noisy, non-monotone per-checkpoint statistic. Examples: block095r seed 1 went 0.95 -> 0.98 -> 0.86; block09 scored 0.980 / 0.926 on two seeds. FT forgets mostly after 1.0M, while Stack climbs 0.6 -> 0.95. 'Retention >= 0.98 in every seed' with 4 seeds x 256 episodes can be decided by luck. Offline drift proxies rank-correlate only -0.53 to -0.82 with sim retention, so they cannot replace sim evals. (6) Chains: each old skill adds 4,096 rows, so the Cholesky grows as O(M^3) and the null space shrinks. (7) The 'self' anchor variant (new-skill states, LwF-style) cannot protect Pick-only states such as goals in the air; expect it to leak.
verdicts.fixes: (a) Project the raw gradient before Adam with the same rows, then project the realised step again (one extra c/alpha solve); keep step-only as an ablation. (b) Damp the restore with step halving or Levenberg-Marquardt, and accept it only if held-out old drift falls. Add the new head's outputs on the current b_obs as equality rows so the restore leaves the new skill unchanged, and log the KL it induces in the new policy. (c) For chains, truncate K to the directions holding 99.99% of its trace (about 500-1,300 of 4,096 per skill); keep the Cholesky in fp64. (d) Compare at matched new-skill success and at a fixed budget past t90 (e.g. 3M). Report retention at 0.5x / 1x / 1.5x t90 with 1,024 episodes. CHEAPEST DECISIVE EXPERIMENT: about 3 GPU-h on Pick->StackCubeNarrow, today's protocol, 4 seeds. Arms: FN-PPO (gradient + step projection, damped restore), FN without restore, restore-only (FT plus a damped GN restore each iteration), block09g (already queued on haha-a), distill/KL-replay at the parent's best coefficient (queued), and FT monitor. GO if FN-PPO's t90 <= 1.25x FT, mean retention >= 0.98 with no seed below 0.95, and it beats restore-only and the best distill arm on retention at equal speed. KILL if restore-only ties it or t90 > 2.2M. BASELINES the paper needs: FT; head-only; FT-N (a separate full copy: retention 0.992 at FT speed, 100% params); LoRA-per-skill r=16; PNN (new column + laterals); PackNet; EWC; L2-SP; KL/BC replay on bank states; LwF on new states; GPM/Adam-NSCL with gradient projection (gpm095g); the Kronecker block with gradient projection; joint multi-task PPO as the upper bound.
